expert.content:
Recommended path and the Java advantage

• Learn Dart fundamentals first, then Flutter widgets, state management, navigation and REST API integration. Reuse your existing Spring Boot backend instead of building a second one for mobile: the same REST endpoints, DTOs and Spring Security rules serve the web app and the Flutter app.
• Java developers adapt quickly: Dart is class-based, statically typed and null-safe, with generics, interfaces, async/await and a familiar syntax. The new ideas are the widget tree (UI as nested constructor calls), immutability of widgets, and state management.
• Build one real app as you progress: a JavaSchoolLab learner app with login, course list, lesson view, progress sync and push notifications.

interviewQA: What is the best order to learn Flutter for a Spring Boot backend?

Dart fundamentals, widgets and layouts, stateless vs stateful widgets, state management (Riverpod or BLoC), navigation, forms, REST and JSON with Dio, authentication with secure storage, local database for offline use, notifications, testing/performance and finally Android deployment.
Do you need a separate backend for the Flutter app?
No. A Spring Boot REST API with JWT/session authentication can serve the web, Flutter and any other client. Only mobile-specific endpoints (device tokens, push registration) need to be added.

topics.name: Introduction to Flutter

beginner.content:
What is Flutter?

• Flutter is Google's open-source UI toolkit for building natively compiled applications for mobile, web, and desktop from a single codebase.
• It uses the Dart programming language and renders every pixel itself via the Skia/Impeller graphics engine, instead of relying on native platform widgets - which is why a Flutter app looks and behaves identically on Android and iOS.
• Everything in Flutter is a Widget - text, padding, buttons, even the whole app itself. Widgets are composed together to build the UI, and Flutter rebuilds only the parts of the widget tree that actually change.

Why Flutter?

1. Single Codebase: Write once, deploy to Android, iOS, Web, Windows, macOS, and Linux.
2. Hot Reload: See code changes reflected in the running app in under a second, without losing app state.
3. Native Performance: Compiles to native ARM/Intel machine code (AOT) for release builds - no JavaScript bridge like some cross-platform frameworks.
4. Rich Widget Library: Material Design (Android-style) and Cupertino (iOS-style) widgets ship out of the box.

intermediate.content:
StatelessWidget vs StatefulWidget

• StatelessWidget: immutable - once built, it never changes. Use it for UI that doesn't depend on any mutable state (e.g. a static label, an icon).
• StatefulWidget: paired with a State object that CAN change over the widget's lifetime. Calling setState() tells Flutter "something changed, rebuild me" - Flutter then efficiently re-renders only the affected subtree.

topics.name: Widgets & Layout Basics

beginner.content:
Building Layouts with Widgets

Flutter layout is built by composing widgets. The two most fundamental layout widgets are:
• Row - arranges children horizontally.
• Column - arranges children vertically.

Other common layout widgets: Container (box model - padding, margin, decoration), Stack (overlapping children), Expanded/Flexible (share available space), ListView (scrollable list).

topics.name: State Management with Provider

beginner.content:
Why State Management?

setState() works fine for small, local state, but it doesn't scale: it can't share state between distant widgets without passing data down through many constructors ("prop drilling"). Provider is one of the most common Flutter state-management packages - it makes an object available to any widget below it in the tree, and rebuilds only the widgets that actually read that object.

intermediate.content:
context.watch() vs context.read()

• context.watch<T>(): subscribes this widget to rebuilds whenever T changes - use it inside build().
• context.read<T>(): reads the value once without subscribing to rebuilds - use it inside callbacks (onPressed, etc.) where you don't need the widget itself to rebuild.

topics.name: Navigation & Routing

beginner.content:
Navigating Between Screens

Flutter manages screens with a stack of routes via the Navigator widget. Navigator.push() adds a new screen on top of the stack; Navigator.pop() removes the current screen and returns to the previous one.

topics.name: Working with APIs (http + FutureBuilder)

beginner.content:
Calling a REST API

The http package makes network requests, which are inherently asynchronous (they return a Future). FutureBuilder is a widget that rebuilds itself based on the state of a Future - loading, error, or data.

topics.name: Introduction, Architecture and Comparisons

beginner.content:
What Flutter is

• Flutter is Google's open-source UI toolkit for building natively compiled apps for mobile (Android, iOS), web, desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux) and embedded devices from one Dart codebase.
• It does not use the platform's native widgets. Flutter draws every pixel itself with its own rendering engine (Impeller, previously Skia), so an app looks and behaves the same on every device and runs at 60/120 fps.
• Apps are built from widgets: small, immutable descriptions of part of the UI, composed into a tree. Dart is compiled AOT (ahead of time) to native ARM code for release builds and JIT for the fast development loop (hot reload).

intermediate.content:
Flutter architecture: three layers

LayerContentsLanguage
FrameworkWidgets, Material/Cupertino, rendering, animation, gestures, foundationDart
EngineImpeller/Skia graphics, Dart runtime, text layout, platform channelsC/C++
EmbedderPlatform-specific host (Android, iOS, Windows...): window, input, event loopJava/Kotlin, ObjC/Swift, C++
• Three trees: the Widget tree (immutable configuration you write), the Element tree (the live instances, managing lifecycle and state) and the RenderObject tree (layout and painting). When state changes, Flutter rebuilds the affected widgets, diffs them against the element tree and updates only what changed.

expert.content:
Flutter vs React Native vs native Android

AspectFlutterReact NativeNative Android (Kotlin/Java)
LanguageDartJavaScript/TypeScriptKotlin / Java
UI approachOwn engine draws all pixelsNative widgets via a bridge/JSINative views (Compose/XML)
Consistency across platformsIdenticalPlatform-native look, may differOne platform only
PerformanceNear native (AOT)Good; JS runtimeBest, full platform access
Code sharing~95% (mobile, web, desktop)~85-90%None across platforms
Dev speedHot reload, one codebaseFast refresh, web skills reuseSlower: two apps for two platforms
New platform APIPlugin or platform channelNative moduleImmediate
Best forBranded, custom-UI apps; small teamsTeams strong in React/JSPlatform-specific, hardware-heavy apps
• For a learning platform with one backend and a small team, Flutter gives Android and iOS (and later web) from one codebase.

interviewQA: What is Flutter and how is it different from React Native?

Flutter is Google's UI toolkit using Dart; it ships its own rendering engine and draws every widget itself, so UI is identical on all platforms. React Native uses JavaScript and renders through native platform widgets.
What are the three trees in Flutter?
The Widget tree (immutable UI description), the Element tree (live instances that hold state and manage updates) and the RenderObject tree (layout and painting).
What is AOT vs JIT compilation in Flutter?
During development Dart runs JIT, enabling hot reload; release builds are compiled AOT to native machine code for fast startup and performance.

topics.name: Dart, Flutter SDK Installation, CLI and Project Structure

beginner.content:
Install the Flutter SDK

• Dart is bundled with Flutter. Requirements: Windows/macOS/Linux, Git, an IDE (Android Studio or VS Code with the Flutter and Dart plugins), the Android SDK (via Android Studio) and, for iOS, a Mac with Xcode.
• Steps: download the SDK from docs.flutter.dev, extract it, add flutter/bin to PATH, run flutter doctor and fix every item it lists (Android licences: flutter doctor --android-licenses).
• Test on an Android emulator (AVD Manager), the Windows/Chrome targets, or a real phone with USB debugging.
codeExamples:
# verify the installation
flutter --version
flutter doctor -v                      # checks SDK, Android toolchain, IDE plugins, connected devices
flutter doctor --android-licenses      # accept SDK licences

# devices
flutter devices
flutter emulators
flutter emulators --launch Pixel_8_API_35

# create and run
flutter create --org com.javaschoollab --platforms=android,ios javaschoollab_app
cd javaschoollab_app
flutter run                            # picks the connected device/emulator
flutter run -d chrome                  # run as a web app

expert.content:
Project structure and pubspec.yaml

• lib/main.dart is the entry point (main() calls runApp). pubspec.yaml declares the app metadata, dependencies, assets and fonts. android/, ios/, web/ hold platform hosts; test/ unit and widget tests; integration_test/ device tests; analysis_options.yaml lint rules.
• Organise lib/ by feature, not by type: each feature has its own data, domain and presentation folders.

│  ├─ app.dart                        # MaterialApp.router, theme
│  ├─ core/                           # theme, router, http client, constants, utils
│  └─ features/
│     ├─ auth/        {data, domain, presentation}
│     ├─ courses/     {data, domain, presentation}
│     └─ profile/

├─ integration_test/
├─ assets/ images/ fonts/
├─ android/  ios/  web/

interviewQA: What does flutter doctor do?
It checks your installation: Flutter SDK, Android toolchain and licences, Xcode, IDE plugins and connected devices, and reports what needs fixing.
What is pubspec.yaml?
The project manifest: name, version, SDK constraints, dependencies, dev dependencies, assets and fonts. flutter pub get resolves it into pubspec.lock.
Why organise code by feature?
Keeping each feature's data, domain and UI together makes the app easier to navigate, test and scale than grouping all screens, models and services by type.

topics.name: Widgets, the Widget Tree and Hot Reload vs Hot Restart

beginner.content:
Everything is a widget

• A widget is an immutable description of part of the UI: structure (Row, Column), visuals (Text, Image), layout helpers (Padding, Center), interaction (GestureDetector, ElevatedButton) and even app-wide data (Theme, MediaQuery).
• You compose UI by nesting widgets. A widget with one child uses child:; one with several uses children: [...].
• Two kinds: StatelessWidget (depends only on its constructor arguments) and StatefulWidget (owns mutable State).

intermediate.content:
Hot reload vs hot restart vs full restart

Hot reloadHot restartFull restart (stop/run)
SpeedSub-secondSecondsSlowest
App stateKeptLost (back to initial)Lost
What it doesInjects changed code into the running VM and rebuilds the widget treeReloads all code and re-runs main()Rebuilds and reinstalls the app
Shortcut (terminal)rRquit and flutter run
Use forUI tweaks, build() changesChanges to main(), global variables, initState, enums, static fieldsNative code, new plugins, pubspec assets/permissions
• Hot reload does not re-run initState or global initialisers, so a change to them needs a hot restart. Adding a package or editing AndroidManifest.xml/Info.plist needs a full restart.

expert.content:
Reading the widget tree and DevTools

• BuildContext is a handle to a widget's position in the tree. Theme.of(context), Navigator.of(context) and MediaQuery.of(context) look up the tree from that position.
• The Flutter Inspector in DevTools shows the widget tree, lets you select widgets on the device and shows layout constraints and sizes; debugPaintSizeEnabled draws layout bounds.
• Use const widgets wherever possible: Flutter reuses them and skips rebuilding.

interviewQA: What is a widget?
An immutable description of part of the user interface. Widgets are composed into a tree; Flutter turns them into elements and render objects to lay out and paint the screen.
Hot reload vs hot restart?

Hot reload injects changed code and rebuilds widgets while keeping app state; hot restart reloads all code and re-runs main(), losing state. Use restart for changes to main, initState or global/static initialisers.
What is BuildContext?
A reference to a widget's location in the widget tree, used to look up inherited data (Theme, MediaQuery, Navigator, providers) from ancestors.

topics.name: Dart Basics: Variables, final vs const, Operators, Control Flow and Functions

beginner.content:
Variables and types

• Dart is statically typed, null-safe and class-based. Core types: int, double, num, String, bool, List, Set, Map, Runes, Symbol, Object, dynamic (avoid), and records (int, String). Null is its own type.
• var infers the type; String name = 'Asha' declares it explicitly; late delays initialisation; everything is an object, even numbers and functions.
• Strings use single or double quotes; interpolation '$name' or '${a + b}'; multi-line with triple quotes; raw strings r'\n'.

intermediate.content:
final vs const

• final: assigned once at runtime; the value may be computed when the program runs (final now = DateTime.now();). The variable cannot be reassigned, but a final list's contents can still change.
• const: a compile-time constant; the value must be known at compile time. const objects are canonicalised (one shared instance) and deeply immutable: const [1, 2] cannot be modified.
• In Flutter use const constructors for widgets: they are created once and never rebuilt, a key performance tool.
• static const for class constants; late final for lazily initialised values.

expert.content:
Operators, control statements and functions

• Operators: arithmetic (+ - * / ~/ %; / always gives a double, ~/ integer division), comparison, logical, bitwise, cascade .., null-aware ?? ??= ?., spread ..., type tests is, is!, as.
• Control: if/else, ternary, for, for-in, while, do-while, break/continue, switch (Dart 3 switch expressions and patterns), collection if/for inside list literals.
• Functions are objects: named parameters {required String x, int y = 1}, positional optional [int z = 0], arrow => for one expression, closures, higher-order functions, typedef.

interviewQA: final vs const in Dart?

final is assigned once at runtime; const is a compile-time constant that is deeply immutable and canonicalised. Use const for known values and const widget constructors; final for values computed at runtime.
What are named parameters?
Parameters declared in braces that callers pass by name, optionally marked required, with defaults. They make calls readable: greet(name: "Asha", greeting: "Hi").
What is the cascade operator?
.. calls several methods or sets fields on the same object and returns that object, e.g. StringBuffer()..write("a")..write("b").

topics.name: Lists, Sets, Maps and Null Safety

beginner.content:
Collections

• List (ordered, indexed, duplicates allowed): [1, 2, 3]; Set (unique, unordered): {1, 2}; Map (key to value): {'a': 1}. Give element types: <String>[], <int, String>{}.
• Functional methods: map, where (filter), reduce, fold, any, every, firstWhere, expand, take/skip, sort, toList(). map/where are lazy iterables: call toList().
• Spread ... and ...?, collection if/for, and immutable List.unmodifiable/const.

intermediate.content:
Null safety

• Since Dart 2.12 types are non-nullable by default: String name can never be null; String? name can. The compiler proves that nullable values are checked before use, eliminating most null-pointer errors.
• Tools: ?. (safe call), ?? (default), ??= (assign if null), ! (assert non-null: throws if wrong, use sparingly), type promotion after a null check, late (promise to initialise before use), required named parameters.
• For fields, a null check promotes only local variables, not mutable fields: copy to a local first.

expert.content:
late, patterns and defensive habits

• late variables are initialised on first access (lazy) or before use; reading an unset late throws LateInitializationError. Use for expensive values (late final x = compute();) and for values set in initState.
• Dart 3 patterns test and destructure in one step: if (value case String s) ..., if (json case {'name': String n}), switch on sealed types.
• Habits: avoid ! when you can restructure; model absence in the type (User?) instead of sentinel values; use Optional-like sealed classes for results; validate JSON at the boundary.

interviewQA: What is null safety in Dart?
Types are non-nullable by default (String) and become nullable only with ? (String?). The compiler enforces null checks, so most null-reference errors are caught at compile time.
What does the ! operator do?
The null assertion operator tells the compiler a nullable expression is not null; at runtime it throws if the value actually is null, so it should be used sparingly.
What is late used for?
Declaring a non-nullable variable that is initialised after its declaration, or lazily on first access; reading it before it is set throws LateInitializationError.

topics.name: Classes, Inheritance, Abstract Classes, Interfaces, Mixins, Extensions and Generics

beginner.content:
Classes and objects

• Dart classes have fields, constructors, methods, getters/setters, static members. Constructor shorthand: Point(this.x, this.y). Variants: named constructors (Point.origin()), factory constructors (may return cached/subclass instances, e.g. fromJson), const constructors, redirecting constructors and initialiser lists.
• Privacy is per library (file), not per class: a name starting with _ is private to its file.
• Override toString, == and hashCode together; or use records / the equatable package.

intermediate.content:
Inheritance, abstract classes and interfaces

• extends inherits from one class; super calls the parent; @override redefines members; polymorphism: a parent-typed variable calls the subclass method.
• Abstract class: cannot be instantiated; may declare abstract methods and share concrete code.
• Every class defines an implicit interface: implements a class (or abstract class) to promise all its members, with no inherited code; a class can implement many interfaces. Dart 3 adds class modifiers: sealed (exhaustive switch), final, base, interface, mixin class.

expert.content:
Mixins, extensions and generics

• A mixin adds reusable behaviour to a class without inheritance: mixin Logger { void log(String m) => print(m); } and class Service with Logger; restrict with on. Flutter uses mixins heavily (SingleTickerProviderStateMixin, AutomaticKeepAliveClientMixin).
• Extension methods add methods to existing types without modifying them: extension on String { ... }.
• Generics make code reusable and type-safe: List<T>, Future<T>, class Box<T extends num>, generic functions T first<T>(List<T> xs). Dart generics are reified (kept at runtime), unlike Java's erasure.

interviewQA: abstract class vs interface in Dart?

An abstract class cannot be instantiated and can mix abstract members with shared code; classes extend it. Every class also defines an implicit interface that other classes implement, providing only the contract. A class can extend one class and implement many.
What is a mixin?
A reusable block of members that a class adds with the with keyword, enabling code reuse without single-inheritance limits. Flutter uses them for tickers, keep-alive and more.
How do Dart generics differ from Java generics?
Dart generics are reified: type arguments exist at runtime (List<int> is distinguishable from List<String>), whereas Java erases them.

topics.name: Exceptions, Futures, async/await, Streams and Isolates

beginner.content:
Exception handling

• Dart has Exception (recoverable, application-level) and Error (programming bugs: StateError, RangeError, TypeError; do not catch). You can throw any object, but throw Exception subclasses.
• try / on Type catch (e, stackTrace) / finally; rethrow keeps the stack trace; on filters by type. There are no checked exceptions.
• Define custom exceptions and prefer returning typed results (sealed Result) for expected failures.

intermediate.content:
Futures and async/await

• A Future<T> represents a value that will be available later (network, file, database, timer). Mark a function async to return a Future and use await to wait without blocking the UI.
• Errors: try/catch around await, or .catchError. Combine futures with Future.wait([...]) (parallel, like Promise.all), Future.any, .timeout(Duration), .then, .whenComplete.
• Dart is single-threaded with an event loop: futures are scheduled on it; they do not create threads. CPU-heavy work needs an isolate.

expert.content:
Streams and isolates

• A Stream<T> delivers many values over time (user input, WebSocket messages, sensor data, file chunks). Consume with await for or listen (returns a StreamSubscription you must cancel). Producers: async* generators with yield, StreamController, Stream.periodic. Single-subscription streams allow one listener; broadcast streams allow many.
• An isolate is an independent worker with its own memory and event loop; isolates share nothing and communicate by message passing. Use Isolate.run() (or Flutter's compute) for heavy work such as parsing a large JSON, image processing or encryption, so the UI never janks.

interviewQA: Future vs Stream?
A Future completes once with a single value (or error). A Stream emits zero or more values over time and can be listened to, transformed and cancelled.
Does async/await create threads in Dart?
No. Dart runs on a single-threaded event loop; async functions are scheduled on it. True parallelism requires isolates, which have separate memory and communicate via messages.
When should you use an isolate?
For CPU-heavy work (parsing big JSON, image/crypto processing, complex calculations) that would otherwise block the UI thread; use Isolate.run or compute.

topics.name: StatelessWidget, StatefulWidget and the Widget Lifecycle

beginner.content:
StatelessWidget

• A StatelessWidget has no mutable state: its output depends only on constructor arguments and inherited data. Override build(BuildContext) to return the UI. Fields are final; use a const constructor.
• Use it for static/derived UI: labels, cards, list items, screens that only display data supplied by a state manager.

intermediate.content:
StatefulWidget and State

• A StatefulWidget is an immutable widget plus a separate, long-lived State object that holds mutable data. Change state inside setState(() { ... }), which marks the widget dirty and schedules a rebuild.
• Two classes: class Counter extends StatefulWidget with createState(), and class _CounterState extends State<Counter>. The widget's fields are reachable as widget.field.
• Local UI state (a toggle, current tab, text field focus, animation) belongs in a StatefulWidget; shared app state belongs in a state-management solution.

expert.content:
The State lifecycle

MethodWhenTypical use
createStateWidget inserted into the treeCreate the State object
initStateOnce, before the first buildCreate controllers, subscribe to streams, start requests (call super.initState() first)
didChangeDependenciesAfter initState and when an inherited widget it depends on changesRead Theme.of, MediaQuery, providers
buildEvery rebuildReturn the UI (keep it pure and fast)
didUpdateWidgetParent rebuilt with new configurationCompare old and new widget, update controllers
deactivateRemoved from the tree (maybe temporarily)Rarely used
disposePermanently removedDispose controllers, cancel subscriptions and timers
• Use mounted before calling setState after an await.

interviewQA: StatelessWidget vs StatefulWidget?

A StatelessWidget has no mutable state and rebuilds only when its parent gives it new data. A StatefulWidget pairs an immutable widget with a State object that holds mutable data and rebuilds via setState.
Why must you call dispose()?
To release controllers, animation tickers, timers and stream subscriptions owned by the State; otherwise they leak and may call setState on a destroyed widget.
What is the mounted property for?
It tells whether the State is still in the tree. After an await the widget may have been removed, so check mounted before calling setState or using context.

topics.name: MaterialApp, Scaffold, Container, SizedBox, Row, Column, Stack and Expanded

beginner.content:
MaterialApp and Scaffold

• MaterialApp is the root of a Material Design app: it provides theme, routing (home, routes, or MaterialApp.router), localisation and the Navigator. CupertinoApp is the iOS-style equivalent.
• Scaffold is the basic screen layout: appBar, body, floatingActionButton, drawer, bottomNavigationBar, snackBar (via ScaffoldMessenger). Almost every screen is a Scaffold.

intermediate.content:
Container, SizedBox, Row and Column

• Container combines padding, margin, decoration, size, alignment and transform in one widget; prefer the specific widget (Padding, SizedBox, DecoratedBox, ColoredBox, Align) when you need only one thing (cheaper, clearer).
• SizedBox: fixed width/height or a spacer (SizedBox(height: 16)); SizedBox.expand(), SizedBox.shrink().
• Row (horizontal) and Column (vertical) lay out children along the main axis (mainAxisAlignment, mainAxisSize) and the cross axis (crossAxisAlignment). The RenderFlex overflowed error means children exceed the available space: fix with Expanded/Flexible, scrolling, or Wrap.

expert.content:
Stack, Positioned, Expanded and Flexible

• Stack layers children on top of each other; Positioned places a child by top/left/right/bottom relative to the Stack (non-positioned children align by alignment). Use for badges, overlays, image captions, floating buttons.
• Expanded makes a child of a Row/Column/Flex fill the remaining main-axis space; several Expanded children share it by flex ratio. Flexible lets a child be up to the available space (fit: FlexFit.loose) without forcing it to fill. Spacer() is an empty Expanded.
• Never put an unbounded child (a ListView, another Column with Expanded) directly inside a Column without bounding its height: wrap in Expanded or give it a size.

interviewQA: Row vs Column and the two axes?
Row lays children horizontally and Column vertically. The main axis is the direction of layout (mainAxisAlignment); the cross axis is perpendicular (crossAxisAlignment).
Expanded vs Flexible?
Expanded forces a child to fill the remaining main-axis space (shared by flex ratio). Flexible lets the child be at most that big and by default does not force it to fill.
What causes "RenderFlex overflowed by N pixels"?
Children of a Row/Column need more space than available. Fix with Expanded/Flexible, a scrollable parent (ListView, SingleChildScrollView), Wrap, or smaller content.

topics.name: ListView, GridView, Text, Image, Buttons, Cards, Dialogs, AppBar and NavigationBar

beginner.content:
ListView and GridView

• ListView is a scrollable list. ListView(children: [...]) builds everything at once (small lists); ListView.builder builds items lazily as they scroll into view (long or infinite lists); ListView.separated adds dividers.
• GridView: GridView.count(crossAxisCount: 2) and GridView.builder with a gridDelegate (SliverGridDelegateWithFixedCrossAxisCount / ...MaxCrossAxisExtent).
• Use stable keys for items that reorder/delete. Nest a list inside a Column only with Expanded or shrinkWrap: true (slow for long lists).

intermediate.content:
Text, images, buttons and icons

• Text: style: TextStyle(...) or Theme.of(context).textTheme.headlineSmall, maxLines, overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis, Text.rich(TextSpan(...)) for mixed styles.
• Image: Image.asset (declare in pubspec.yaml), Image.network (use cached_network_image in real apps; set loadingBuilder/errorBuilder), fit: BoxFit.cover.
• Buttons (Material 3): FilledButton, ElevatedButton, OutlinedButton, TextButton, IconButton, FloatingActionButton; onPressed: null disables a button. Icons: Icon(Icons.home).

expert.content:
Cards, dialogs, AppBar and NavigationBar

• Card: elevated, rounded surface (Card.filled, Card.outlined in Material 3). Dialogs: showDialog + AlertDialog, showModalBottomSheet, showDatePicker; they return a Future with the result. SnackBar for brief messages.
• AppBar (title, leading, actions, bottom: TabBar), SliverAppBar for collapsing bars. NavigationBar (Material 3 bottom bar with NavigationDestinations), NavigationRail (tablets/desktop), Drawer.
• Do not use BuildContext across async gaps without checking context.mounted.

interviewQA: Why use ListView.builder?
It builds only the items currently visible (and a small cache) as the user scrolls, so long or unlimited lists stay fast and memory-light; the plain ListView builds all children immediately.
How do you show a dialog and get a result?
Call showDialog<T> with an AlertDialog; Navigator.pop(context, value) closes it and the awaited Future returns value (null if dismissed).
Why check context.mounted after await?
The widget may have been removed while waiting; using its BuildContext afterwards can throw or act on a stale tree.

topics.name: Custom Widgets and Responsive UI

beginner.content:
Building reusable widgets

• Extract UI into your own widgets (classes, not helper methods that return widgets) to get const optimisation, separate rebuilds, a testable unit and clear names. Design them with a small, typed API: required named parameters, sensible defaults, callbacks (VoidCallback, ValueChanged<T>), and a child/builder for flexibility.
• Use composition over inheritance: build a PrimaryButton from a FilledButton, not by subclassing.

intermediate.content:
Responsive UI basics

• Phones, tablets, foldables and the web have very different sizes. Design responsively: use flexible layouts (Expanded, Wrap, GridView with max extent), avoid fixed pixel sizes, and switch layouts at breakpoints (compact below 600 dp, medium 600-840, expanded above 840).
• Tools: MediaQuery.sizeOf(context), LayoutBuilder (parent constraints), OrientationBuilder, FractionallySizedBox, AspectRatio, FittedBox, text scaling (textScaler).
• Test with different devices, orientations, large font sizes and in split-screen.

expert.content:
Accessibility and keeping widgets small

• Accessibility: add Semantics labels to icons/images, use tooltip on icon buttons, minimum 48x48 dp tap targets, sufficient contrast, support large text (avoid fixed heights for text) and screen readers (TalkBack/VoiceOver).
• Keep build() small: split big widgets into smaller classes; keep logic out of build; pass only the data a widget needs so unrelated changes do not rebuild it.
• Prefer const, avoid creating controllers or doing work in build, and use ListView.builder for long lists.

interviewQA: Why create widget classes instead of helper methods?
Classes can be const, get their own element/State, rebuild independently, are testable and show up in DevTools; methods that return widgets rebuild with their parent and prevent these optimisations.
LayoutBuilder vs MediaQuery?
MediaQuery gives the size of the whole screen/window; LayoutBuilder gives the constraints of the widget's parent, which is more accurate for components inside panes or split screens.
What is a good minimum touch target size?
About 48x48 dp (Material guideline), so buttons and icons are easy to tap for all users.

topics.name: Padding, Margin, Alignment and Constraints-Based Layout

beginner.content:
Padding, margin and alignment

• Padding adds space inside a widget's box; margin is space outside (a Container's margin, or wrap with Padding). Use EdgeInsets.all, .symmetric(horizontal, vertical), .only, .fromLTRB, and EdgeInsetsDirectional for right-to-left languages.
• Alignment: Center, Align(alignment: Alignment.bottomRight), mainAxisAlignment/crossAxisAlignment in Row/Column, AlignmentDirectional, Text(textAlign: ...). Use an 8-dp spacing scale (4, 8, 16, 24, 32) for consistency.

intermediate.content:
The layout algorithm: constraints go down, sizes go up

• Flutter layout rule: "Constraints go down. Sizes go up. Parent sets position." A parent passes BoxConstraints (min/max width and height) to each child; the child picks a size within them and reports it; the parent positions the child.
• Tight constraints force an exact size (min = max); loose constraints allow any size up to max; unbounded means max is infinity (inside a scroll view or a Row/Column main axis).
• Consequences: a child cannot choose its own size or position; a widget with a fixed size ignored inside a tight parent (SizedBox(width: 50) inside a SizedBox.expand still fills). Use Center/Align to loosen constraints, ConstrainedBox/SizedBox to set them.

expert.content:
Common constraint errors and how to fix them

ErrorCauseFix
RenderFlex overflowedRow/Column children larger than available spaceExpanded/Flexible, Wrap, scrolling, shorter content
Vertical viewport was given unbounded heightListView inside Column (infinite height)Wrap the ListView in Expanded or give it a SizedBox/shrinkWrap
BoxConstraints forces an infinite widthExpanded/TextField inside an unbounded Row/ColumnBound the parent, wrap with SizedBox/Expanded
Incorrect use of ParentDataWidgetExpanded outside Row/Column/Flex, Positioned outside StackPlace it as a direct child of the right parent
A widget ignores its sizeParent passes tight constraintsWrap in Center/Align
• Debug layouts with the Flutter Inspector ("Layout Explorer") and debugPaintSizeEnabled.

interviewQA: What is the main Flutter layout rule?
Constraints go down, sizes go up, and the parent sets the position: a parent gives each child min/max constraints, the child chooses a size within them, and the parent places it.
Why does a ListView inside a Column throw an unbounded height error?
A Column gives its children unbounded height, and a ListView tries to be as tall as its content, which cannot be computed. Wrap it in Expanded or give it a fixed size (or shrinkWrap for short lists).
Why is my Container size ignored?
Its parent passed tight constraints that force a size. Wrap the Container in Center or Align so the constraints become loose and your size can apply.

topics.name: BoxDecoration, Themes, Dark Mode and Custom Fonts

beginner.content:
BoxDecoration

• BoxDecoration (in Container or DecoratedBox) paints background and border: color, gradient (LinearGradient, RadialGradient), border (Border.all), borderRadius, boxShadow, image (DecorationImage), shape: BoxShape.circle.
• Do not set both color on the Container and decoration (error): put the color inside the decoration.

intermediate.content:
Themes and dark mode

• A ThemeData defines the app's look: colorScheme (generate from a seed: ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: ...)), textTheme, component themes (appBarTheme, elevatedButtonTheme, cardTheme, inputDecorationTheme), useMaterial3: true.
• Read it with Theme.of(context): colorScheme.primary, textTheme.titleLarge. Never hard-code colours in widgets; use the scheme so dark mode works.
• Dark mode: give MaterialApp both theme and darkTheme and a themeMode (system, light, dark); let users choose and persist the choice (SharedPreferences) in a provider.

expert.content:
Custom fonts and ThemeExtensions

• Custom fonts: place font files in assets/fonts/, declare them under flutter: fonts: in pubspec.yaml, then set fontFamily in the theme. Or use the google_fonts package (downloads at runtime; bundle fonts for offline apps and for privacy).
• ThemeExtension adds your own design tokens (brand colours, spacing, radii) to the theme with lerp support for animated theme changes.
• Keep a small design system: colours, typography, spacing, radii in one place.

interviewQA: How do you support dark mode in Flutter?
Provide theme and darkTheme to MaterialApp with a themeMode, build both from a ColorScheme, and read colours from Theme.of(context) instead of hard-coding them; persist the user's choice.
Why use ColorScheme.fromSeed?
It generates a harmonious, accessible Material 3 palette (primary, secondary, surface, containers) from one seed colour for both light and dark brightness.
How do you add a custom font?
Add the font files to assets, declare them under flutter: fonts: in pubspec.yaml, and set fontFamily in ThemeData or TextStyle (or use the google_fonts package).

topics.name: MediaQuery, LayoutBuilder, Adaptive UI and Animations Basics

beginner.content:
MediaQuery and LayoutBuilder in practice

• MediaQuery.sizeOf(context) (screen size), .orientationOf, .paddingOf (safe-area insets: notch, status bar), .viewInsetsOf (keyboard height), .textScalerOf, .platformBrightnessOf. Use the specific methods (sizeOf) so the widget rebuilds only when that value changes.
• SafeArea keeps content out of notches and system bars. LayoutBuilder reacts to the parent's constraints.

intermediate.content:
Adaptive UI

• Responsive = adjust to size; adaptive = adjust to platform and input too: bottom bar on phones vs NavigationRail on tablets/desktop; Cupertino look on iOS (Switch.adaptive, CircularProgressIndicator.adaptive, showAdaptiveDialog); mouse hover and keyboard shortcuts on desktop/web; touch targets on mobile.
• Detect the platform with Theme.of(context).platform (not dart:io, which fails on web) and kIsWeb.
• The flutter_adaptive_scaffold package switches between bottom navigation, rail and drawer automatically.

expert.content:
Animations and transitions: the basics

• Implicit animations animate automatically when a property changes: AnimatedContainer, AnimatedOpacity, AnimatedAlign, AnimatedPositioned, AnimatedSwitcher, AnimatedCrossFade, TweenAnimationBuilder. Set duration and curve; no controller needed.
• Page transitions: MaterialPageRoute by default; custom with PageRouteBuilder or GoRouter's CustomTransitionPage; Hero animates a shared element between screens.
• Keep animations short (150-400 ms), respect "reduce motion" (MediaQuery.disableAnimationsOf) and avoid animating layout-heavy widgets (animate Transform/Opacity instead).

interviewQA: Responsive vs adaptive design?

Responsive adapts layout to available size (breakpoints, flexible widgets). Adaptive also adapts to platform and input: native-looking controls on iOS/Android, navigation rail vs bottom bar, keyboard and mouse support on desktop.
Why use MediaQuery.sizeOf instead of MediaQuery.of(context).size?
sizeOf subscribes the widget only to size changes, so it does not rebuild for unrelated MediaQuery changes such as the keyboard or text scale.
What is an implicit animation?
A widget like AnimatedContainer that automatically animates from the old to the new value when its properties change, using a duration and curve, without an AnimationController.

topics.name: setState, InheritedWidget, ChangeNotifier and ValueNotifier

beginner.content:
What is state?

• State is any data that can change while the app runs and affects what the UI shows. Flutter is declarative: UI = f(state). You change the state and Flutter rebuilds the UI.
• Ephemeral (local) state belongs to one widget (current tab, a toggle, text field content, animation progress): use StatefulWidget + setState. App state is shared by many screens or survives them (logged-in user, cart, settings, fetched data): use a state-management solution.
• setState(() { ... }) marks the widget dirty and schedules a rebuild of that widget and its subtree; keep the rebuilt subtree small.

intermediate.content:
InheritedWidget: the foundation

• An InheritedWidget exposes data to all descendants without passing it through constructors. Descendants call context.dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType<T>() (usually wrapped in T.of(context)) and are rebuilt automatically when the widget's data changes (updateShouldNotify).
• Theme, MediaQuery, Navigator and Provider/Riverpod are built on this idea. You rarely write one by hand, but it explains how Theme.of(context) works.

expert.content:
ChangeNotifier and ValueNotifier

• ChangeNotifier is a plain Dart class with notifyListeners(): a simple observable model. Listen with ListenableBuilder/AnimatedBuilder (built in) or via Provider's ChangeNotifierProvider.
• ValueNotifier<T> is a ChangeNotifier holding one value (value = x notifies); rebuild just the part that cares with ValueListenableBuilder: excellent for small, local reactive values without a package.
• Always dispose() notifiers you create; keep notifiers free of BuildContext and UI code so they are testable.

interviewQA: What is the difference between ephemeral and app state?

Ephemeral state is local to one widget (a toggle, current tab) and fits StatefulWidget/setState. App state is shared across screens or must persist (user, cart, settings) and belongs in a state-management solution.
What is InheritedWidget?
A widget that makes data available to all descendants and rebuilds those that depend on it when the data changes. Theme, MediaQuery and Provider are built on it.
ChangeNotifier vs ValueNotifier?
ChangeNotifier is a general observable class that calls notifyListeners() after changes; ValueNotifier is a ChangeNotifier that holds a single value and notifies when it is assigned.

topics.name: Provider and Riverpod

beginner.content:
Provider

• Provider (package provider) wraps InheritedWidget with a simple API: ChangeNotifierProvider at the top of the tree, then context.watch<T>() (rebuild on change), context.read<T>() (one-off access, use in callbacks), context.select (rebuild only when a selected field changes), Consumer<T>.
• Good for small/medium apps. Limits: dependency on BuildContext, runtime (not compile-time) errors for missing providers, awkward for async data and combining providers.

intermediate.content:
Riverpod

• Riverpod (by the author of Provider) is compile-safe, context-independent and testable. State lives in providers declared as global (but immutable) variables inside a ProviderScope. Widgets become ConsumerWidget/ConsumerStatefulWidget and use ref.watch (rebuild), ref.read (callbacks), ref.listen (side effects like snackbars).
• Provider types: Provider (computed/read-only), StateProvider (simple value), NotifierProvider/AsyncNotifierProvider (state + methods; modern), FutureProvider/StreamProvider (async data with built-in loading/error states), .family (parameters), .autoDispose (free state when unused), riverpod_generator annotations.

expert.content:
Riverpod in a real feature: AsyncNotifier and testing

• AsyncNotifier loads data in build() and exposes mutation methods (add, remove) that update state with AsyncValue.guard, giving loading/error handling for free; combine with optimistic updates.
• Overrides make testing trivial: ProviderScope(overrides: [courseRepositoryProvider.overrideWithValue(fake)]) in widget tests, or ProviderContainer for unit tests without widgets.
• Rules: do not ref.watch inside callbacks (use read); do not store providers' state in widgets; keep UI dumb.

interviewQA: Provider vs Riverpod?

Riverpod is the successor by the same author: providers are global and compile-safe, independent of BuildContext, support async (FutureProvider/AsyncNotifier), autoDispose, families and easy overrides for tests, so it avoids Provider's runtime errors.
ref.watch vs ref.read vs ref.listen?
watch rebuilds the widget when the provider changes (use in build); read gets the current value once (use in callbacks); listen runs a side effect (navigation, snackbar) on change without rebuilding.
What is AsyncValue?
A Riverpod type representing loading, data or error for async providers, consumed with when/switch so the UI handles all three states explicitly.

topics.name: BLoC, Cubit, GetX, Best Practices and Choosing a Solution

beginner.content:
Cubit

• BLoC (Business Logic Component) separates UI from logic with streams: the UI sends events/calls methods, the logic emits states, the UI rebuilds from them. Package: flutter_bloc (+ bloc, equatable).
• Cubit is the simple form: a class extending Cubit<State> with methods that call emit(newState). Use it for most features.
• Model the state as an immutable class or a sealed class hierarchy (Initial, Loading, Loaded, Failure) and switch over it exhaustively. UI: BlocProvider (create), BlocBuilder (rebuild), BlocListener (side effects), BlocConsumer, context.read.

intermediate.content:
BLoC with events, and GetX

• A full Bloc receives events (on<LoadCourses>(handler)) and emits states; it gives traceability (every event is logged by BlocObserver), event transformers (debounce, droppable, restartable via bloc_concurrency) and is common in large teams. More boilerplate than Cubit.
• GetX bundles state management (.obs, Obx, GetxController), navigation without context (Get.to) and dependency injection (Get.put). It is quick to write, but mixes concerns, hides dependencies, uses a lot of "magic" and has had maintenance concerns: prefer Riverpod or BLoC for serious apps; know GetX because you will meet it in existing projects.

expert.content:
Best practices and choosing the right solution

• Best practices: keep UI free of business logic; one source of truth; immutable state (copyWith, freezed, records); rebuild as little as possible (select, small widgets); handle loading/error/empty explicitly; dispose resources; inject repositories (testable); do not use global mutable singletons; do not put BuildContext in state classes; separate UI state from server state/cache.
• A layered structure: presentation (widgets + controllers/notifiers/cubits) → domain (entities, use cases/repository interfaces) → data (API, database, DTOs).
SolutionStrengthWeaknessChoose when
setStateBuilt in, trivialLocal onlyOne widget's state
ProviderSimple, official-ishContext-bound, runtime errorsSmall/medium apps, existing codebases
RiverpodCompile-safe, async, testable, flexibleNew concepts (refs, families)Most new apps; recommended
BLoC/CubitStrict structure, traceable events, great for big teamsMore boilerplateLarge teams, complex flows, strict architecture
GetXVery little codeMagic, mixes concerns, maintenance riskPrototypes; legacy projects
• For JavaSchoolLab: Riverpod (or BLoC). Pick one, use it consistently, and write the repository layer so the choice stays replaceable.

interviewQA: Cubit vs Bloc?

A Cubit exposes methods that call emit(state) and is simpler. A Bloc receives events and maps them to states through event handlers, which adds traceability and event transformers (debounce, restartable) at the cost of more boilerplate.
Why is GetX often discouraged for large apps?
It mixes state, navigation and DI in a global, implicit way that hides dependencies and hinders testing and maintenance; Riverpod or BLoC give clearer structure.
How do you choose a state-management solution?

Use setState for local state; for app state choose Riverpod (flexible, testable, async-friendly) or BLoC/Cubit (strict structure for big teams); keep the choice behind repositories and be consistent across the app.

topics.name: Navigator, Named Routes, Passing and Returning Data

beginner.content:
Navigator 1.0: the route stack

• Navigator manages a stack of routes (screens). Navigator.push(context, route) adds a screen; Navigator.pop(context) removes the top one (the Android back button and iOS swipe do the same). pushReplacement, pushAndRemoveUntil (clear history after login), popUntil, maybePop.
• MaterialPageRoute builds the platform-appropriate transition. Each screen is a normal widget (usually a Scaffold).

intermediate.content:
Named routes and passing data

• Named routes: MaterialApp(routes: {'/': ..., '/course': ...}) or onGenerateRoute (needed for arguments and unknown routes); navigate with Navigator.pushNamed(context, '/course', arguments: ...). Named routes are simple for small apps but lack type safety and web/deep-link support: GoRouter is recommended for real apps.
• Pass data by constructor: CourseDetailPage(course: course) (type-safe, preferred), or via route arguments read with ModalRoute.of(context)!.settings.arguments.
• Pass an id (and reload from the repository) rather than a large object when the screen can be opened by URL or notification.

expert.content:
Returning data from a screen

• Navigator.push returns a Future that completes when the pushed route is popped; Navigator.pop(context, result) supplies the result. Use it for pickers, confirmations and edit screens.
• Check context.mounted after await. Intercept the back gesture with PopScope (replaces WillPopScope) to warn about unsaved changes.

interviewQA: How do you return data from a screen?
Await Navigator.push<T>(...), which completes with the value passed to Navigator.pop(context, value) on the second screen (null if closed without a result).
Why are named routes not enough for big apps?
They are string-based, lack type safety and typed parameters, and handle deep links and web URLs poorly. GoRouter or Router 2.0 solve this declaratively.
How do you prevent going back with unsaved changes?
Wrap the screen in PopScope with canPop false when dirty, handle onPopInvokedWithResult, ask the user to confirm, then pop manually.

topics.name: GoRouter, Route Guards, Deep Linking and Nested Navigation

beginner.content:
GoRouter basics

• GoRouter (go_router, maintained by the Flutter team) is a declarative, URL-based router built on Navigator 2.0: routes have paths with parameters, the stack is derived from the URL, and it supports deep links, web URLs, redirects, nested navigation and typed routes.
• context.go('/courses/5') navigates (replaces the stack to match the URL); context.push('/courses/5') pushes on top; context.pop(). Path parameters :id via state.pathParameters; query parameters via state.uri.queryParameters; extra passes an object (not restored on web/deep link).

intermediate.content:
Route guards with redirect

• A redirect runs before navigation and returns a new location (or null to continue). Use it as a route guard: send unauthenticated users to /login and authenticated users away from it. Rebuild the router when auth changes with refreshListenable (a ChangeNotifier/stream adapter) or by watching an auth provider.
• Remember the intended destination (?from=/courses/5) and return after login. Role checks (/admin) belong in redirects, but the server must enforce them; client guards are only usability.

expert.content:
Deep linking and nested navigation (ShellRoute)

• Deep links open the app at a specific screen from a URL: Android App Links (https://app.javaschoollab.com/courses/5 verified through assetlinks.json, android:autoVerify="true" intent filter), iOS Universal Links (apple-app-site-association), custom schemes (javaschoollab://). With GoRouter the path simply matches a route; notifications can carry the same path.
• Nested navigation: ShellRoute / StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack keeps a persistent shell (bottom bar) while each tab keeps its own navigation stack and state.
• Test links: adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "https://app.javaschoollab.com/courses/5".

interviewQA: What does GoRouter add over Navigator.push?
Declarative URL-based routing: typed path/query parameters, deep links and web URLs, redirects (guards), nested navigation with shell routes and a consistent back stack derived from the URL.
How do you protect routes in GoRouter?
Use the redirect callback (with refreshListenable or an auth provider) to send unauthenticated users to /login and return them afterwards; the server still enforces authorisation.
What is a StatefulShellRoute?
A shell (such as a bottom navigation bar) around several branches, each preserving its own navigation stack and state when you switch tabs.

topics.name: Bottom Navigation and Tab Navigation

beginner.content:
Bottom navigation

• Material 3 uses NavigationBar with NavigationDestination items (3-5 top-level destinations); older apps use BottomNavigationBar. Keep tab state with IndexedStack (all tabs stay alive) or PageStorageKey/AutomaticKeepAliveClientMixin.
• Each tab often needs its own navigator stack so Back stays inside the tab: use StatefulShellRoute in GoRouter or nested Navigators.
• On wide screens switch to NavigationRail.

intermediate.content:
Tab navigation

• TabBar + TabBarView inside a DefaultTabController (or a TabController with SingleTickerProviderStateMixin) gives swipeable tabs below an AppBar: for sections within one screen (Overview, Lessons, Reviews).
• Preserve a tab's scroll position with AutomaticKeepAliveClientMixin (wantKeepAlive => true) or PageStorageKey.
• Lazy-load heavy tab content; tabs are built when first shown.

expert.content:
Combining navigation patterns

• Typical app: bottom bar for top-level areas → inside a tab a stack (list → detail) → inside a detail screen TabBar sections; modal flows (login, checkout) pushed above the shell with parentNavigatorKey: rootNavigatorKey.
• Handle Android back: from a tab's first screen the back button should go to the first tab, then exit (PopScope).
• Show badges (Badge) for unread counts and set labelBehavior for compact bars.

interviewQA: IndexedStack vs creating pages on demand for tabs?

IndexedStack keeps all tab widgets (and their state/scroll) alive at the cost of memory and upfront build; building on demand saves resources but loses state unless you use keep-alive mixins or storage keys.
How do you keep a separate navigation stack per bottom tab?
Use StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack in GoRouter (each branch has its own stack) or nested Navigator widgets with their own keys.
TabBar vs NavigationBar?
NavigationBar (bottom) switches between top-level destinations of the app; TabBar (usually under the AppBar) switches between sections of one screen.

topics.name: TextField, TextEditingController, Form, GlobalKey and FocusNode

beginner.content:
TextField and TextFormField

• TextField is the basic text input; TextFormField is a TextField that integrates with a Form (validation, save, reset). Configure with InputDecoration (label, hint, prefix/suffix icons, errorText, border), keyboardType, textInputAction, obscureText (password), maxLength, inputFormatters, autofillHints, autocorrect.
• Callbacks: onChanged, onSubmitted, onEditingComplete, onTap.

intermediate.content:
TextEditingController and FocusNode

• A TextEditingController reads and sets the text (controller.text), selection and listens to changes. Create it in initState (or as a field) and always dispose() it. Do not create controllers in build().
• A FocusNode controls and observes keyboard focus: requestFocus(), unfocus(), listen for focus changes (validate on blur), move focus between fields (FocusScope.of(context).nextFocus(), textInputAction + onFieldSubmitted). Dispose it too.
• Dismiss the keyboard on outside tap with GestureDetector(onTap: () => FocusScope.of(context).unfocus()).

expert.content:
Form widget and GlobalKey

• Form groups several TextFormFields (and other FormFields such as DropdownButtonFormField). A GlobalKey<FormState> gives access to the form's state from outside: validate() runs every field's validator and returns true if all pass, save() calls each onSaved, reset() restores initial values.
• autovalidateMode: disabled (default), always, onUserInteraction (best UX: validate after the user touches a field).
• A GlobalKey must be created once per form (keep it in the State, not in build).

interviewQA: TextField vs TextFormField?
TextFormField wraps a TextField as a FormField so it takes part in a Form: validator, onSaved, autovalidateMode and form.validate()/save()/reset(). Plain TextField has no validation integration.
Why must you dispose a TextEditingController?
It holds listeners and resources; if not disposed it leaks memory. Create it in initState (not build) and dispose it in dispose().
What does the GlobalKey<FormState> do?
Gives access to the Form's state from anywhere, so you can call validate(), save() and reset() (for example in a submit button handler).

topics.name: Validation, Dropdowns, Checkboxes, Radio Buttons and Pickers

beginner.content:
Validation

• A validator is a function String? Function(String?): return null when valid or the error message. Put rules in reusable functions and compose them. Match the UX: validate on interaction, show specific messages, focus the first invalid field.
• Also validate on the server and map server errors (400/422) back to fields with InputDecoration.errorText or a form-level message.
• Packages: form_builder_validators, formz; keep simple rules inline.

intermediate.content:
Dropdowns, checkboxes, radio buttons and switches

• DropdownButtonFormField<T> (or Material 3 DropdownMenu<T>): items, value, onChanged, validator. Use an enum or model as T.
• Checkbox/CheckboxListTile: value (bool?), onChanged. Switch/SwitchListTile for on/off settings. Radio/RadioListTile (group with groupValue), or the newer RadioGroup; SegmentedButton for small option sets; FilterChip/ChoiceChip for tags.
• To validate a checkbox (terms accepted) wrap it in a FormField<bool>.

expert.content:
Date and time pickers

• showDatePicker, showTimePicker, showDateRangePicker return a Future with the chosen value (or null if cancelled). Format with the intl package (DateFormat('dd MMM yyyy').format(date)).
• Make a read-only TextFormField that opens the picker on tap so it fits the form and validation.
• Store dates as UTC ISO-8601 strings in JSON and convert to local time for display.

interviewQA: How do you validate a checkbox in a Form?
Wrap it in a FormField<bool> with a validator and a builder that shows the checkbox and the error text; the form's validate() then includes it.
When should validation run?
AutovalidateMode.onUserInteraction gives good UX: each field validates after the user touches it, and the whole form validates on submit; always validate again on the server.
How do you handle dates between Flutter and Spring Boot?
Send and receive ISO-8601 strings (UTC), parse with DateTime.parse and format for display with intl; Spring serialises java.time types as ISO strings when configured.

topics.name: File Upload Forms

beginner.content:
Picking a file or image

• Pick documents with file_picker (FilePicker.platform.pickFiles(type: FileType.custom, allowedExtensions: ['pdf'])) and photos with image_picker (gallery or camera). They return a path/bytes plus name and size.
• Validate before uploading: allowed type, maximum size, count; show a preview (Image.file, file name and size).
• Permissions: gallery access on recent Android/iOS needs the system photo picker or scoped permissions (see Device Features).

intermediate.content:
Uploading with multipart and progress

• Send files as multipart/form-data: with Dio use FormData and MultipartFile.fromFile (streams from disk, so large files do not fill memory); onSendProgress gives progress for a LinearProgressIndicator; CancelToken allows cancel.
• Include other form fields in the same FormData. The Spring Boot side uses @RequestPart MultipartFile file; set spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size.
• Handle failure and retry; for big uploads consider chunked/resumable uploads or pre-signed URLs to object storage.

expert.content:
The upload form UI

• Combine preview, progress, error and a disabled submit button while uploading. Keep the picked file in state; compress images (imageQuality, flutter_image_compress) before upload to save data.
• Do not trust the file name or MIME type on the server; scan and re-validate. Store uploads outside the web root with generated names.

interviewQA: How do you upload a file to a Spring Boot API from Flutter?

Send multipart/form-data using Dio FormData with MultipartFile.fromFile; on Spring use @RequestPart MultipartFile (and set max-file-size). Show progress with onSendProgress and allow cancel with CancelToken.
Why validate file size and type on the client and server?
The client gives instant feedback and saves bandwidth; the server must still validate because clients can be bypassed and MIME types or names can be forged.
Why use MultipartFile.fromFile instead of reading bytes?
It streams the file from disk, so large files do not have to be loaded fully into memory.

topics.name: HTTP Requests, CRUD and JSON Serialization

beginner.content:
HTTP requests with the http package

• Add http (flutter pub add http). http.get(Uri.parse(url)), post, put, patch, delete return a Future<http.Response> with statusCode, body, headers.
• Build URIs safely: Uri.https(host, path, queryParameters) (encodes values). Always set Content-Type: application/json and Accept, and check the status code: the Future completes normally for 4xx/5xx.
• Android emulator reaches your PC's localhost at 10.0.2.2; iOS simulator at localhost; a real phone needs your LAN IP or a deployed server. Plain HTTP on Android 9+ needs usesCleartextTraffic (debug only); Android needs the INTERNET permission in release manifests.

intermediate.content:
CRUD: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE

• Put each resource's calls in one API/repository class, return domain models (not raw JSON) and throw typed exceptions.

expert.content:
JSON serialization and deserialization

• Manual: jsonDecode gives dynamic (Map<String, dynamic>/List); write fromJson factory and toJson methods. Fine for small apps; cast carefully (as String?, (x as num).toDouble()), handle missing/null fields, and parse dates with DateTime.parse.
• Code generation: json_serializable + json_annotation (annotate the class, run dart run build_runner build); freezed adds immutable models, copyWith, equality and unions; dart_mappable is an alternative. Use @JsonKey(name: 'course_id') for naming differences; Spring's Jackson uses camelCase by default.
• Parse large JSON off the UI thread with compute()/Isolate.run.

interviewQA: Why must you check statusCode with the http package?
The Future completes successfully for any HTTP response, including 404 and 500; only network failures throw. You must inspect statusCode and convert errors to exceptions yourself.
How do you reach a localhost Spring Boot server from the Android emulator?
Use http://10.0.2.2:8080 (the emulator's alias for the host machine); a real device needs the computer's LAN IP or a deployed HTTPS server.
Manual JSON parsing vs json_serializable?
Manual code is fine for small models but error-prone as they grow. json_serializable/freezed generate fromJson/toJson (and immutability, copyWith, equality), reducing boilerplate and typos.

topics.name: Dio, Error Handling, Loading States and Pagination

beginner.content:
Dio vs http

• Dio is a powerful HTTP client: base options (baseUrl, timeouts, headers), interceptors, automatic JSON encoding/decoding, FormData/multipart with progress, cancellation (CancelToken), retries (via interceptors), certificate pinning hooks and a typed DioException. The http package is smaller and enough for simple needs.
• Create one configured Dio instance (provided through Riverpod/Provider/get_it) and reuse it. Set validateStatus if you want non-2xx to return instead of throw (default: non-2xx throws a DioException of type badResponse).

intermediate.content:
Error handling

• DioException.type: connectionTimeout, sendTimeout, receiveTimeout, badResponse (has response.statusCode and body), cancel, connectionError (offline/DNS), badCertificate, unknown.
• Convert them once in the data layer (interceptor or repository) to your own sealed failure types (NetworkFailure, Unauthorized, Validation(fields), ServerFailure, NotFound) so the UI never sees Dio. Show friendly messages; log technical details.
• Retry idempotent GETs on timeouts/5xx with exponential backoff (dio_smart_retry or a small interceptor).

expert.content:
Loading states and pagination

• Every request screen has four states: loading, success, empty, error (with a retry button). Use AsyncValue (Riverpod), a sealed state (BLoC) or FutureBuilder. Show skeletons/shimmer instead of blank screens; pull-to-refresh with RefreshIndicator.
• Pagination: use page/size (or cursor) parameters (?page=2&size=20; Spring Pageable returns content, totalPages, last). Load the next page when the user scrolls near the end (ScrollController listener or ListView.builder itemBuilder index check); show a bottom loader; guard against duplicate requests and stop when last is true. The infinite_scroll_pagination package wraps this pattern.

interviewQA: Dio vs http package?
Dio adds interceptors, base options, timeouts, multipart with progress, cancellation and typed exceptions; http is a minimal client. Use Dio for real apps that need auth headers, retries and logging.
Where should DioException be converted to user-facing errors?
In the data layer (an interceptor or repository wrapper) into your own failure types, so the UI shows friendly messages and never depends on Dio.
How do you implement infinite scroll?
Track page, hasMore and loading flags; when the list nears its end request the next page, append items, show a bottom loader, prevent duplicate requests and stop when the server says last.

topics.name: Spring Boot REST API Integration and Authentication

beginner.content:
One backend for web and mobile

• Reuse the existing JavaSchoolLab Spring Boot API: same endpoints, DTOs and Spring Security. Add mobile-specific needs only where required (device token registration for push, versioned endpoints, mobile-friendly pagination).
• Contract: generate an OpenAPI document with springdoc-openapi and generate Dart clients/models (openapi-generator with the dart-dio generator, or chopper/retrofit) to avoid hand-written drift.
• Use consistent JSON: camelCase, ISO-8601 dates, { status, message, errors } error bodies, and API versioning (/api/v1) because installed apps cannot be updated instantly.

intermediate.content:
Authentication flow with Spring Security

• Typical mobile flow: POST /api/auth/login with credentials → server returns a short-lived access token (JWT) and a refresh token → the app stores them in secure storage → a Dio interceptor attaches Authorization: Bearer ... → on 401 the interceptor calls /api/auth/refresh once, retries the original request, otherwise logs out.
• Expose AuthState (unknown, authenticated(user), unauthenticated) from an auth provider; GoRouter redirects use it. On start the app restores the session from storage and calls /api/me.
• Never log tokens or passwords; use HTTPS everywhere.

expert.content:
Environment, networking details and testing against Spring

• Pass the base URL with --dart-define=API_URL=https://api.javaschoollab.com and read it with String.fromEnvironment; use flavours (dev/staging/prod) for different backends.
• CORS does not apply to mobile apps (it is a browser rule); it matters only for Flutter Web. Android needs HTTPS in production (cleartext blocked) and the INTERNET permission.
• Test the integration with the Spring Boot server running locally (10.0.2.2), use MockWebServer-style fakes (http_mock_adapter) in tests, and run contract checks against the OpenAPI spec in CI.

interviewQA: How does the Flutter app authenticate with Spring Security?

Log in to receive a short-lived access token and a refresh token, store them in secure storage, attach the access token with an interceptor, refresh once on 401, and log out if refresh fails; Spring validates tokens and enforces roles.
Does CORS affect Flutter mobile apps?
No. CORS is enforced by browsers, so it affects only Flutter Web. Mobile apps call the API directly, but still need HTTPS and the INTERNET permission.
How do you point the app at different environments?
Use --dart-define values (String.fromEnvironment) or flavours to set the API base URL per build, never hard-coding URLs or secrets in source.

topics.name: Futures, async/await, FutureBuilder and Error Handling

beginner.content:
Futures in Flutter

• Flutter UI runs on one thread; anything slow (network, disk, database) must be async so frames keep rendering at 60/120 fps. A Future<T> completes later with a value or an error; await pauses the function, not the UI.
• Future.wait runs several in parallel; Future.delayed for delays; .timeout(); Completer bridges callback APIs to Futures; unawaited() marks fire-and-forget.
• Do not call async work inside build(): it would restart on every rebuild.

intermediate.content:
FutureBuilder

• FutureBuilder<T> builds UI from a Future's AsyncSnapshot (connectionState, hasData, hasError, data, error). Create the Future once (in initState or a field), never inline in build, or each rebuild restarts the request.
• Handle all branches: waiting, error, data, empty. For app-wide data prefer a state-management solution (Riverpod FutureProvider), which also caches and shares results.

expert.content:
Error handling in async code

• try/catch around await; on SpecificException; always use finally to reset loading flags. A Future error that nobody handles is reported as an unhandled exception.
• Global handlers: FlutterError.onError (framework errors in build/layout) and PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError (async errors) feed a crash reporter (Crashlytics/Sentry); runZonedGuarded was the older way.
• Do not swallow errors silently; log with context and show a user-friendly message. Check mounted before using setState/context after await.

interviewQA: Why must the Future for FutureBuilder not be created inside build?
build runs on every rebuild, so a Future created inline would restart the request each time, causing repeated calls and flicker. Create it once in initState or a provider.
What does await do to the UI?
Nothing blocking: it suspends only the async function; the event loop keeps rendering frames and handling input, then resumes the function when the Future completes.
How do you catch uncaught async errors globally?
Set FlutterError.onError for framework errors and PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError for async errors, and send them to a crash reporting service.

topics.name: Streams, StreamBuilder, StreamController and Real-Time Data

beginner.content:
Streams and StreamBuilder

• A Stream<T> emits a sequence of values over time. Sources: Stream.periodic, generators (async*/yield), StreamController, plugin APIs (connectivity, location, Firebase snapshots, WebSocket).
• StreamBuilder<T> rebuilds on each event from an AsyncSnapshot; it subscribes and unsubscribes automatically. Provide initialData to avoid a loading flash. Like FutureBuilder, create or hold the stream once.
• Stream methods: map, where, asyncMap, distinct, take, transform, debounceTime (rxdart).

intermediate.content:
StreamController

• StreamController lets you push values: controller.add(value), addError, close(). Single-subscription (default) allows one listener; broadcast (StreamController.broadcast()) allows many but drops events with no listeners. rxdart's BehaviorSubject replays the latest value to new listeners.
• Expose only controller.stream from a class, keep the controller private, and close it in dispose. Cancel every StreamSubscription you create with listen.

expert.content:
Real-time data handling

• WebSocket (web_socket_channel): channel.stream for incoming messages and channel.sink.add to send. Spring Boot supports WebSocket/STOMP or Server-Sent Events (SseEmitter, Flux) for live progress, chat and notifications.
• Real-world needs: reconnect with backoff, heartbeat/ping, authentication (token in the connection request), message parsing with typed events, handling background/foreground and offline, de-duplicating events, and merging live updates into cached state (Riverpod StreamProvider).
• Firestore/Realtime Database offer streams out of the box (see Firebase section).

interviewQA: Future vs Stream in Flutter UI?
FutureBuilder renders a single async result; StreamBuilder rebuilds on every value of a stream (live data, sensors, WebSocket). Both need the Future/Stream created once and outside build.
Single-subscription vs broadcast stream?
A single-subscription stream allows one listener and buffers events until it listens; a broadcast stream allows many listeners but events are lost when nobody is listening.
What must a real-time client handle besides receiving messages?
Reconnection with backoff, authentication, heartbeats, parsing and de-duplicating events, offline/background transitions and cleaning up subscriptions and controllers.

topics.name: Concurrency with Isolates and Cancellation Strategies

beginner.content:
Isolates for heavy work

• All Dart code runs in an isolate with its own heap and event loop; the UI isolate must stay free. Move CPU-heavy work (parsing a multi-MB JSON, image processing, encryption, sorting huge lists, database migrations) to another isolate so frames are not dropped (jank).
• Isolate.run(() => ...) (Dart 3) runs a function and returns its result; compute(fn, arg) is the Flutter equivalent. Arguments and results are copied (or transferred as TransferableTypedData); closures can capture only sendable values; plugins/platform channels may be unavailable in background isolates (use RootIsolateToken/BackgroundIsolateBinaryMessenger).
• Do not isolate trivial work: spawning costs a few milliseconds.

intermediate.content:
Long-lived isolates and message passing

• For ongoing work (a background indexer, a worker pool) spawn an isolate with Isolate.spawn and talk through SendPort/ReceivePort. Send plain data (numbers, strings, lists, maps, records, SendPort); share nothing.
• Packages: flutter_isolate (plugins in isolates), squadron, worker_manager (pools), workmanager (OS background tasks, different mechanism).

expert.content:
Cancellation strategies

• Dart Futures cannot be cancelled natively. Strategies: ignore stale results (compare a request id/version before applying), Dio CancelToken (aborts the HTTP request), StreamSubscription.cancel(), Timer.cancel(), CancelableOperation/CancelableCompleter (async package), Riverpod's ref.onDispose + ref.cancel pattern (cancel in-flight work when the provider is disposed), rxdart's switchMap (latest wins), and killing isolates (isolate.kill).
• Cancel work when the user leaves the screen or types a new query; avoid updating disposed widgets (mounted).

interviewQA: When should you use an isolate?
For CPU-bound work that would block the UI thread, such as parsing large JSON, image processing or encryption. Use Isolate.run or compute; do not use them for I/O, which is already asynchronous.
Can a Dart Future be cancelled?
Not directly. Cancel the underlying operation (Dio CancelToken, subscription.cancel, Timer.cancel), use CancelableOperation, or ignore stale results with a request id.
Do isolates share memory?
No. Each has its own heap; they communicate by passing messages through ports, with data copied (or transferred) between them.

topics.name: SharedPreferences, Secure Storage and File Storage

beginner.content:
SharedPreferences

• shared_preferences stores small key-value pairs (bool, int, double, String, List<String>) in platform storage (Android SharedPreferences, iOS NSUserDefaults). Perfect for settings: theme mode, language, onboarding done, last tab.
• Not encrypted and not for large or relational data, secrets or tokens. Use the async API (SharedPreferencesAsync/SharedPreferencesWithCache in newer versions) and wrap it in a small repository so storage can change.

intermediate.content:
Secure storage

• flutter_secure_storage keeps secrets in the platform's secure store: Android Keystore (EncryptedSharedPreferences) and iOS Keychain. Use it for access/refresh tokens, API keys the user entered, encryption keys for local databases.
• Options: AndroidOptions(encryptedSharedPreferences: true), IOSOptions(accessibility: KeychainAccessibility.first_unlock). Remember iOS Keychain items can survive app uninstall; clear on first launch if needed. Values are strings; small data only.
• Never put tokens in SharedPreferences, logs or source code.

expert.content:
File storage

• path_provider gives directories: getApplicationDocumentsDirectory() (user data, backed up), getApplicationSupportDirectory() (app files), getTemporaryDirectory() (cache, may be cleared), getExternalStorageDirectory() (Android).
• Read/write with dart:io File: writeAsString, readAsString, writeAsBytes, openWrite (streams); use jsonEncode for structured data. Keep large media on disk and store paths in the database.
• On Android 10+ scoped storage limits access outside the app's folders; use the system pickers/MediaStore (gal, saver_gallery) to save to the gallery. Not available on Flutter Web (dart:io).

interviewQA: SharedPreferences vs secure storage?
SharedPreferences stores plain key-value settings, unencrypted, for non-sensitive data. Secure storage uses the Android Keystore/iOS Keychain to protect secrets such as tokens.
Where should you store a downloaded file?

In the application documents (persistent) or temporary/cache directory from path_provider, depending on whether it must survive; use the system pickers or MediaStore to save to shared storage on Android 10+.
Why wrap storage in a repository class?
It hides the plugin, centralises keys and types, and makes it easy to test and replace the storage mechanism later.

topics.name: SQLite, Drift, Hive and Isar

beginner.content:
SQLite with sqflite

• SQLite is a relational database in a single file on the device: tables, SQL, indexes, transactions, joins. Package sqflite (Android/iOS/macOS) or sqlite3 + sqlite3_flutter_libs. Create tables in onCreate, migrate in onUpgrade with a version number.
• Use parameterised queries (? placeholders, whereArgs) to avoid injection and quoting bugs; wrap multi-step writes in transaction or batch; add indexes for searched columns; keep DB work off the UI path (it is already async).

intermediate.content:
Drift (type-safe SQLite)

• Drift (formerly Moor) is a reactive, type-safe persistence library on top of SQLite: you declare tables in Dart, it generates data classes and a query API, supports SQL and a Dart query builder, compile-time checked SQL, joins, transactions, schema migrations with verification, DAOs, and reactive streams (watch() emits when data changes), plus web support. Recommended for JavaSchoolLab's offline cache (Java developers will feel at home: tables ≈ JPA entities, DAOs ≈ repositories).

expert.content:
Hive, Isar and choosing a store

• Hive: fast, pure-Dart key-value/NoSQL boxes; simple objects with type adapters; good for caches and small collections. The original is in maintenance; hive_ce is a maintained fork.
• Isar: fast embedded NoSQL database with typed collections, indexes, queries and reactive watchers; check the package's maintenance status before committing (the original author has slowed down; forks such as isar_community exist).
