interviewQA: Why choose Drift over raw sqflite?
Drift is type-safe and generates code, offers compile-time checked queries, reactive streams (watch), DAOs and verified schema migrations, reducing runtime SQL mistakes.
What is a database migration?
A versioned change to the schema (adding a column or table) that runs when the installed database is older than the app's schemaVersion, so existing user data is preserved.
Which local store should hold auth tokens?
Neither a database nor SharedPreferences; use flutter_secure_storage (Keystore/Keychain) so tokens are encrypted by the platform.

topics.name: Caching, Offline Support and Local Database Synchronization

beginner.content:
Caching strategies

• A cache keeps data close to the UI so screens open instantly and work with a bad network. Common policies: cache-first (show cached data, refresh in the background: stale-while-revalidate), network-first (try the network, fall back to cache), cache-then-network (emit cache, then fresh), with a TTL and a max size.
• Single source of truth: the UI observes the local database; the repository refreshes it from the API. The UI never reads the network directly. Images: cached_network_image; HTTP: dio_cache_interceptor.

intermediate.content:
Offline support

• Detect connectivity with connectivity_plus (a hint only: "connected" does not mean the server is reachable; real errors are the truth) and show an offline banner.
• Offline reads: from the local database. Offline writes: apply to the database immediately (optimistic), add the action to an outbox queue table (pending_actions: id, type, payload JSON, createdAt, attempts), and show a "pending sync" indicator. Make actions idempotent (client-generated UUIDs) so a retry never duplicates.
• Decide per feature what works offline: lessons already downloaded, notes, progress; not payments or live chat.

expert.content:
Local database synchronization

• Push: process the outbox oldest-first, send each action (with Idempotency-Key: clientId), delete on success, increment attempts and back off on failure, drop or flag after N failures; stop on 401 (refresh/login). Run when connectivity returns, on app resume and periodically (WorkManager on Android for background sync).
• Pull: fetch changes since the last sync (GET /api/sync?since=2026-10-20T10:00:00Z or an incrementing version/ETag), merge into the database in one transaction, store the new lastSyncedAt. Use soft deletes (deleted flag) so deletions propagate.
• Conflicts: choose a policy: last-write-wins (timestamp), server-wins, field-level merge, or ask the user. Add a version column (Spring @Version) so the server can reject stale updates with 409.

interviewQA: What is the single source of truth pattern?
The UI reads only from the local database; the repository refreshes the database from the network. Data flows network → database → UI, which gives instant screens and offline behaviour.
How do you make offline writes safe to retry?
Queue each action with a client-generated UUID and send it as an idempotency key, so the server can detect and ignore duplicates when the same action is retried.
How can sync conflicts be resolved?
With a policy such as last-write-wins, server-wins or field-level merge, using version numbers/timestamps (optimistic locking, HTTP 409) to detect conflicting edits, or by asking the user.

topics.name: Login, Registration, JWT, Token Refresh and Secure Token Storage

beginner.content:
Login and registration screens

• Build login/registration with a Form, proper keyboard types, autofillHints (password managers), show/hide password, loading state, server-error mapping and "forgot password". Disable the button while submitting; never reveal whether an email exists on login failures ("Invalid email or password").
• Spring Security side: POST /api/auth/register (hash passwords with BCrypt/Argon2), POST /api/auth/login → { accessToken, refreshToken, user }, POST /api/auth/refresh, POST /api/auth/logout, GET /api/me.

intermediate.content:
JWT and token refresh

• A JWT (header.payload.signature) carries claims (sub, roles, exp). It is signed, not encrypted: never put secrets in it; the server verifies it. The app may decode the payload (jwt_decoder) to read exp and roles for UI decisions only.
• Use short-lived access tokens (5-15 min) and a refresh token (days/weeks), rotated on every use with reuse detection on the server; revoke on logout and password change.
• Refresh proactively (shortly before exp) or reactively on 401; make sure only one refresh runs at a time (queue concurrent requests with a QueuedInterceptor or a shared Future) and retry the failed request once. If refresh fails: clear tokens and route to login.

expert.content:
Secure token storage and Spring Security integration

• Store tokens in flutter_secure_storage only (Keystore/Keychain). Keep the access token also in memory to avoid reading storage on every request. Clear everything on logout. Never log tokens.
• Spring Security (Java): stateless resource server validating the JWT (oauth2ResourceServer(jwt) or a custom filter), CORS not required for mobile, password hashing with BCryptPasswordEncoder, rate limiting for login, account lockout, optional MFA. Return 401 for missing/invalid tokens and 403 for insufficient rights.
• Consider OAuth2/OIDC with PKCE (flutter_appauth) for social login (Google) or a corporate IdP instead of building credentials handling yourself.

interviewQA: Why use short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens?
If an access token leaks it is useful only briefly; the long-lived refresh token is stored more carefully, rotated on each use and can be revoked, giving both security and a smooth user experience.
Why must only one token refresh run at a time?

Several requests failing with 401 together would each try to refresh; with rotating refresh tokens the second attempt would use an already-used token and trigger revocation. Share one in-flight refresh and retry the others.
Is a JWT encrypted?
No. It is signed, so it can be verified, but its payload is only base64url-encoded and readable. Never put secrets in it and always verify it on the server.

topics.name: Biometric Authentication, Certificate Validation and Network Security

beginner.content:
Biometric authentication

• local_auth shows the system fingerprint/face/PIN prompt: canCheckBiometrics, isDeviceSupported, authenticate(localizedReason: ..., options: AuthenticationOptions(biometricOnly: false, stickyAuth: true)). It answers "is this the device owner?"; it does not replace server login.
• Typical use: protect re-opening the app, show sensitive screens, or unlock stored tokens (store the refresh token in secure storage with biometric protection; or require biometrics before using it). Fall back to the device PIN, handle "no biometrics enrolled" and lockouts.
• Android needs USE_BIOMETRIC and the activity must extend FlutterFragmentActivity; iOS needs NSFaceIDUsageDescription.

intermediate.content:
Certificate validation and pinning

• Always use HTTPS and never disable certificate validation (badCertificateCallback = (cert, host, port) => true is a serious vulnerability that makes man-in-the-middle attacks trivial). Fix certificate problems on the server (a complete chain, valid hostname, not expired).
• Certificate pinning makes the app accept only your server's certificate/public key (or its CA), even if a device trusts a rogue CA: pin the public key hash (SPKI) with a backup pin and a rotation plan (pinning to an expiring leaf breaks the app when the certificate renews). Implement with Dio's IOHttpClientAdapter.createHttpClient + SecurityContext, or packages (http_certificate_pinning, dio_http2_adapter).
• Android's Network Security Config (res/xml/network_security_config.xml) can disable cleartext and pin domains declaratively.

expert.content:
Network and app security checklist

• Secure API communication: HTTPS/TLS 1.2+, short timeouts, validate responses, send tokens only to your API host (not third parties), no secrets in URLs/query strings, no sensitive data in logs (strip in release), avoid print in release.
• Do not embed secrets in the app: API keys with write power, signing keys, DB passwords are extractable from the binary. Anything shipped is public; use server-side secrets and restrict keys (package name + SHA-1, per-API restrictions).
• Hardening: --obfuscate --split-debug-info for release builds (slows reverse engineering, not security); detect rooted/jailbroken devices (flutter_jailbreak_detection) for high-risk apps; FLAG_SECURE to block screenshots on sensitive screens (flutter_windowmanager/no_screenshot); clear clipboard; disable Android backup of sensitive data (android:allowBackup="false").
• Keep dependencies updated (flutter pub outdated, advisories), and follow OWASP MASVS.

interviewQA: Does biometric authentication replace server-side login?
No. It proves the device owner is present; it is used to unlock the app or stored credentials after a normal login, while the server still authenticates via tokens.
What is certificate pinning?

Configuring the app to accept only a known server certificate or public key, so connections intercepted with a rogue but device-trusted certificate authority are rejected. It needs backup pins and a rotation plan.
Why shouldn't you embed API secrets in a mobile app?
The binary can be decompiled and strings extracted easily; any secret shipped in the app is effectively public. Keep secrets on the server and issue short-lived, restricted tokens.

topics.name: Role-Based Access Control

beginner.content:
Roles and permissions

• RBAC: users have roles (STUDENT, INSTRUCTOR, ADMIN) that grant permissions (course:create, user:ban). Put roles/permissions in the user object (from /api/me) or the JWT claims, and model them as an enum/set in Dart.
• In Flutter use roles to shape the UI: hide admin menus, disable edit buttons, route guards for /admin. This is usability, not security: the Spring Boot API must enforce every rule with @PreAuthorize and ownership checks.

intermediate.content:
Route guards by role and the server as the authority

• Add a role check to the GoRouter redirect for protected areas and show a "403" page; keep menus consistent with the routes.
• Server: @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')"), method security, and ownership checks (a student may read only their own progress; never trust an id sent by the client). Return 401 (not authenticated) or 403 (not allowed) and let the app react centrally (logout on 401, "no access" on 403).
• Re-fetch the user (roles) after login, on app resume and after a 403, since roles may change on the server.

expert.content:
Testing and designing permissions

• Unit-test the permission logic (user.can(...)) and widget-test that restricted widgets do not appear for the wrong role (ProviderScope overrides with a fake user).
• Prefer permissions over role names in UI checks (can('course:delete')) so roles can be reshuffled on the server without app updates.
• Default deny: show nothing until the user is loaded; treat unknown roles as no access.

interviewQA: Are role checks in the Flutter app a security measure?
No. They only tailor the UI. The server must authenticate and authorise every request, because client code can be modified or bypassed.
Why prefer permissions to role names in the UI?
Permissions describe capabilities (course:delete), so roles can change on the server without changing app code; role names couple the app to the role design.
What do 401 and 403 mean?
401: not authenticated (missing or invalid token); 403: authenticated but not allowed. The app logs out or refreshes on 401 and shows a no-access message on 403.

topics.name: CustomPainter and Animations: Implicit, Explicit, AnimationController and Hero

beginner.content:
CustomPainter

• CustomPaint + CustomPainter draw directly on a Canvas: lines, paths, arcs, shapes, text, images, gradients. Override paint(Canvas canvas, Size size) and shouldRepaint(old) (return true only when inputs change). Use for charts, progress rings, signatures, game-like visuals.
• Paint configures colour, stroke width, style (fill/stroke), StrokeCap, shader. Wrap in RepaintBoundary to isolate repaints; keep paint cheap and allocation-free.

intermediate.content:
Implicit and explicit animations

• Implicit (easy): AnimatedContainer, AnimatedOpacity, AnimatedAlign, AnimatedPositioned, AnimatedSwitcher, TweenAnimationBuilder: change a value and Flutter animates to it (duration, curve).
• Explicit (full control): an AnimationController (needs a vsync ticker: with SingleTickerProviderStateMixin; always dispose) produces a value 0.0 to 1.0 over a duration; Tween maps it to any range/type, CurvedAnimation adds a curve; drive widgets with AnimatedBuilder or ready-made transitions (FadeTransition, ScaleTransition, SlideTransition, RotationTransition). Control: forward(), reverse(), repeat(), stop(), animateTo().
• Staggered animations use Interval curves on one controller.

expert.content:
Hero animations and performance

• A Hero flies a shared widget between two routes: wrap the widget on both screens in Hero(tag: sameTag, child: ...) (tags must be unique per screen and equal across them). Use for thumbnails that expand into a detail image; customise with flightShuttleBuilder.
• Animation performance: animate Transform/Opacity (cheap, no re-layout) rather than size/padding where possible; use AnimatedBuilder's child to avoid rebuilding static parts; RepaintBoundary around heavy animated areas; avoid saveLayer (Opacity on big trees); profile with DevTools. Consider Lottie (lottie) or Rive for designer-made animations.
• Respect MediaQuery.disableAnimationsOf(context) for users who reduce motion.

interviewQA: Implicit vs explicit animations?

Implicit animations (AnimatedContainer etc.) animate automatically when a property changes; explicit animations use an AnimationController (with a vsync ticker) and tweens for full control: repeat, reverse, sequencing and syncing several animations.
Why must an AnimationController be disposed?
It holds a Ticker that fires every frame; if not disposed it leaks and throws errors after the widget is removed.
How does a Hero animation work?
Two widgets on different routes share the same Hero tag; during the route transition Flutter flies the widget from its old position and size to the new one.

topics.name: Slivers and CustomScrollView

beginner.content:
What are slivers?

• A sliver is a portion of a scrollable area that builds and lays out lazily. CustomScrollView composes several slivers into one scroll: collapsing app bars, headers that pin, lists and grids in the same scroll, parallax effects. ListView and GridView are just convenient wrappers around slivers.
• Slivers: SliverAppBar (pinned, floating, expandedHeight, flexibleSpace), SliverList/SliverList.builder, SliverGrid, SliverToBoxAdapter (any normal widget), SliverPadding, SliverFillRemaining, SliverPersistentHeader (custom sticky header), SliverFixedExtentList, SliverMainAxisGroup.

intermediate.content:
Sticky headers and nested scrolling

• SliverPersistentHeader with a SliverPersistentHeaderDelegate creates pinned section headers or a search bar that sticks (pinned: true); the delegate defines minExtent, maxExtent and build(context, shrinkOffset, overlapsContent).
• NestedScrollView + TabBarView keeps a collapsing header above tabs that each scroll (use SliverOverlapAbsorber/NestedScrollView.sliverOverlapAbsorberHandleFor). ScrollController reads offset (parallax, "back to top" button, pagination triggers). RefreshIndicator works with slivers via CustomScrollView physics; Cupertino: CupertinoSliverRefreshControl.
• Do not nest a ListView with shrinkWrap: true inside another scroll view for long content (it builds everything): use slivers instead.

expert.content:
Sliver pitfalls and performance

• Unbounded errors: a RenderBox (a normal widget) cannot be placed directly in CustomScrollView.slivers: wrap it in SliverToBoxAdapter; conversely a sliver outside a scroll view fails. Use SliverFillRemaining(hasScrollBody: false) for an empty/footer state that fills the leftover space.
• Laziness: prefer SliverList.builder/SliverGrid.builder and avoid shrinkWrap; give items Keys; set itemExtent/prototypeItem where heights are fixed. Put expensive headers in SliverPersistentHeader with a cheap shouldRebuild.
• Pull-to-refresh and pagination: wrap the CustomScrollView in RefreshIndicator, add a SliverToBoxAdapter loader at the end and trigger the next page from a NotificationListener<ScrollNotification> or a ScrollController near maxScrollExtent.

interviewQA: What is a sliver?

A lazily built portion of a scrollable area. CustomScrollView combines slivers (app bars, lists, grids, headers) into one coordinated scroll, enabling collapsing and sticky effects that a single ListView cannot do.
SliverList vs ListView?
ListView is a convenience widget that wraps a single SliverList in a scroll view; use SliverList inside CustomScrollView when you need to mix it with other slivers in one scroll.
Why avoid shrinkWrap ListViews inside scroll views?
shrinkWrap forces the list to compute the size of all its children, losing lazy building and hurting performance; slivers keep everything lazy.

topics.name: Platform Channels and FFI

beginner.content:
Platform channels

• Flutter cannot call Android (Kotlin/Java) or iOS (Swift) APIs directly. A platform channel passes asynchronous messages between Dart and the host app: MethodChannel (call a method, get a result), EventChannel (a stream of events from native to Dart, e.g. sensors), BasicMessageChannel. Both sides use the same channel name. Data types are serialised with the standard codec (null, bool, int, double, String, Uint8List, List, Map).
• Use it when no plugin exists. Prefer an existing plugin; to share your channel code, create a plugin package (flutter create --template=plugin). Use Pigeon to generate type-safe channel code.

intermediate.content:
FFI (Foreign Function Interface)

• dart:ffi calls C/C++ (and Rust, via C ABI) libraries directly and synchronously from Dart, without a message-passing layer: good for performance-critical code, existing native libraries (image codecs, crypto, ML, SQLite) and sharing one implementation across platforms.
• Steps: write/obtain the native library, expose a C interface, load it (DynamicLibrary.open / DynamicLibrary.process), look up functions (lookupFunction), convert types with ffi (Pointer, Utf8, calloc/malloc and free what you allocate). ffigen generates bindings from C headers; flutter_rust_bridge for Rust; native assets/hooks (package:native_assets_cli) for building.
• FFI calls block the calling isolate: run long ones in a background isolate.

expert.content:
Channels vs FFI, and plugin/package guidance

Platform channelFFI
TargetPlatform SDK (Kotlin/Swift): permissions, system servicesC/C++/Rust libraries
CallsAsynchronous messages (serialised)Direct, synchronous calls
OverheadHigher per callVery low
Typical useBluetooth, biometrics, custom OS integrationsAlgorithms, codecs, crypto, existing native libs
Cross-platform reuseWrite per platformOne native implementation
• Before writing either, search pub.dev (likes, pub points, maintenance, platform support, null safety). Wrap third-party plugins behind your own interface so you can swap or mock them.
• Test channel code with TestDefaultBinaryMessengerBinding / setMockMethodCallHandler; keep native handlers small and well-typed (Pigeon).

interviewQA: MethodChannel vs EventChannel?
MethodChannel performs a request/response call to native code and returns a Future; EventChannel exposes a stream of events from native to Dart (sensors, battery changes).
When would you choose FFI over a platform channel?
When calling C/C++/Rust code for performance or reuse across platforms. FFI is direct and synchronous; channels are asynchronous message passing to platform SDKs.
Why wrap a plugin behind an interface?
So features depend on your abstraction, making the plugin replaceable and the code testable with fakes.

topics.name: Background Processing, Notifications, Deep Linking and App Lifecycle

beginner.content:
App lifecycle management

• The app moves through states: resumed (foreground, interactive), inactive (transition/incoming call), hidden, paused (background), detached. Observe them with WidgetsBindingObserver.didChangeAppLifecycleState or AppLifecycleListener.
• Use it to: pause timers/streams/camera/video when backgrounded, save drafts, refresh data and token on resume, lock the app (biometrics), reconnect sockets, stop location updates. The OS may kill a background app at any time: persist important state (RestorationMixin, database).

intermediate.content:
Background processing

• The OS limits background work to save battery. Options: WorkManager (workmanager package): deferrable, guaranteed periodic/one-off tasks (sync every 15+ minutes, upload when on Wi-Fi) using Android WorkManager and iOS BGTaskScheduler; foreground service with a persistent notification (music, tracking, long uploads: flutter_foreground_task); push notifications (data messages) to wake the app for fresh content; isolates only while the app is alive.
• Background callbacks run in a separate isolate without UI: initialise plugins and storage inside the callback (@pragma('vm:entry-point') top-level function). Keep tasks short, idempotent, and respect battery constraints (Constraints(networkType: NetworkType.connected)).

expert.content:
Local notifications and deep links from notifications

• flutter_local_notifications shows notifications generated by the app (reminders: "Study time!", download complete): initialise with platform settings, create an Android notification channel (importance, sound), request the POST_NOTIFICATIONS permission on Android 13+ and iOS, schedule with zonedSchedule (timezone package) and handle taps (onDidReceiveNotificationResponse) to navigate to a screen using the payload (a route like /courses/5).
• Remote push is covered in Device Features/Firebase. Both should feed the same navigateFromPayload(path) function that calls router.go(path): also the entry for deep links.
• Handle three entry states for taps: app terminated (get the launch details), background, foreground.

interviewQA: How do you run work in the background in Flutter?

With WorkManager for deferrable periodic tasks, a foreground service for long visible work, or push notifications to wake the app; callbacks run in a separate isolate without UI and must initialise what they need.
Why observe the app lifecycle?
To pause or release resources when backgrounded, save state before the OS kills the app, refresh data and tokens when it resumes and re-lock sensitive screens.
How do you open a screen from a notification tap?
Put a route or id in the notification payload and, in the tap handler (and launch details for the terminated case), call the router (router.go(path)).

topics.name: Camera, Gallery, Image Picker, File Downloads and Uploads

beginner.content:
Permissions: the common pattern

• Sensitive features (camera, location, microphone, contacts, notifications, Bluetooth) need runtime permission and a manifest/Info.plist entry. Use permission_handler: Permission.camera.request() returns granted, denied, permanentlyDenied, restricted, limited.
• Best practice: ask in context (when the user taps "Take photo"), explain why first (rationale dialog), handle denial gracefully, and send the user to Settings (openAppSettings()) when permanently denied.

intermediate.content:
Camera and gallery

• image_picker: pickImage(source: ImageSource.camera|gallery), pickMultiImage, pickVideo - uses the system camera/photo picker (no camera permission needed on modern Android for the picker; the camera intent may need it). camera package: live preview (CameraController, CameraPreview, takePicture, startVideoRecording) for custom camera UIs, QR/document scanning (mobile_scanner).
• Reduce size at pick time (maxWidth, imageQuality); show a preview; handle null (cancelled); dispose CameraController and manage lifecycle (pause on background).

expert.content:
File downloads and uploads

• Downloads: Dio().download(url, savePath, onReceiveProgress: ...) streams to disk (resume with Range headers); save to the app documents directory, then open with open_filex/open_file or share. For public downloads on Android 10+ use the MediaStore API (gal, saver_gallery, media_store_plus). Show a notification and progress; large/background downloads: background_downloader.
• Uploads: multipart with Dio (see the upload form lesson), progress, cancel, retry, compress before sending; on Spring Boot store with generated names and validate size/type.
• Verify integrity (checksum) for important files; handle low storage and network drops.

interviewQA: How should you ask for a runtime permission?
In context when the feature is used, with a short explanation first; handle denial gracefully, and when it is permanently denied direct the user to app settings with openAppSettings().
image_picker vs camera package?
image_picker launches the system camera or photo picker and returns a file (simple). The camera package gives a live preview and full control for custom camera UIs, scanners and video recording.
How do you save a downloaded image to the gallery on Android 10+?
Use MediaStore through a plugin such as gal or saver_gallery instead of writing to arbitrary external paths, because scoped storage restricts direct file access.

topics.name: Location, GPS, Bluetooth and Sensors

beginner.content:
Location services and GPS

• geolocator reads the position: Geolocator.isLocationServiceEnabled(), checkPermission()/requestPermission(), getCurrentPosition(locationSettings: LocationSettings(accuracy: LocationAccuracy.high)), getLastKnownPosition() (fast), getPositionStream() (tracking with distanceFilter). geocoding converts coordinates to addresses.
• Manifest: ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION/ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION (Android); NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription (iOS). Background location needs extra permission and a foreground service, and heavy store review: avoid unless essential. Choose lowest accuracy that works to save battery.

intermediate.content:
Bluetooth (BLE)

• flutter_blue_plus (BLE central role): scan (FlutterBluePlus.startScan), connect (device.connect()), discover services, read/write/subscribe to characteristics (GATT), listen to connectionState. Needs Bluetooth permissions (Android 12+: BLUETOOTH_SCAN, BLUETOOTH_CONNECT; location on older versions; iOS NSBluetoothAlwaysUsageDescription).
• Handle: adapter off, permission denied, device out of range, reconnect, MTU, timeouts; always stop scanning and disconnect when done. Classic Bluetooth (SPP) needs other packages. Not available on iOS simulators.

expert.content:
Sensors

• sensors_plus streams accelerometer, user accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer: accelerometerEventStream(samplingPeriod: SensorInterval.normalInterval). Use for shake detection, step-like motion, tilt UI, compass (with flutter_compass); pedometer, light, proximity via other plugins.
• Sensors drain battery: choose a coarse sampling interval, cancel subscriptions when the screen is hidden, and throttle processing. Always handle devices without a given sensor (errors on the stream).

interviewQA: How do you save battery when using GPS?
Use the lowest accuracy that satisfies the feature, a distanceFilter for streams, getLastKnownPosition when possible, stop streams when not needed and avoid background location unless essential.
What is a BLE characteristic?
A GATT data point exposed by a Bluetooth Low Energy device inside a service. You can read, write or subscribe to notifications on it to exchange data.
Why cancel sensor subscriptions in dispose?
Sensor streams run continuously and consume battery and CPU; leaving them subscribed after the screen is gone wastes resources and may call setState on a disposed widget.

topics.name: Share, Clipboard, Connectivity Monitoring and Contacts

beginner.content:
Share and Clipboard

• share_plus opens the native share sheet: Share.share(text, subject: ...), Share.shareXFiles([XFile(path)]) (e.g. a certificate PDF). Share a deep link (https://app.javaschoollab.com/courses/5) so recipients open the right screen.
• Clipboard (built in): Clipboard.setData(ClipboardData(text: ...)), Clipboard.getData(Clipboard.kTextPlain). Show a confirmation SnackBar. Do not read the clipboard silently (privacy; Android 12+/iOS show a toast); avoid copying secrets and clear sensitive clipboard content.

intermediate.content:
Connectivity monitoring

• connectivity_plus: Connectivity().checkConnectivity() and onConnectivityChanged (a List<ConnectivityResult>: wifi, mobile, ethernet, vpn, bluetooth, none). It reports the interface, not real internet access: use internet_connection_checker_plus (pings) or treat request failures as the truth.
• Show an offline banner, pause/queue syncing while offline, retry when back online, and let users keep using cached content. Provide the status app-wide via a Riverpod StreamProvider.

expert.content:
Contacts integration

• flutter_contacts (or contacts_service successors): request READ_CONTACTS (Android) / NSContactsUsageDescription (iOS), then FlutterContacts.getContacts(withProperties: true) or the system contact picker (FlutterContacts.openExternalPick()) which needs no permission and returns only the chosen contact (preferred: privacy-friendly).
• Typical use: invite friends, referral. Treat contacts as sensitive personal data: ask only when needed, hash phone numbers before sending to your server, state the purpose, and comply with privacy rules (GDPR/DPDP); Play Store requires a clear declaration.

interviewQA: Does connectivity_plus tell you that the internet works?
No. It reports the active network interface (wifi, mobile, none), not real internet reachability; verify with an actual request or an internet checker and treat request failures as the truth.
Why prefer the system contact picker?
It returns only the contact the user chooses without requiring the READ_CONTACTS permission, which is more privacy-friendly and easier to get through store review.
How do you share a link that opens a specific screen?
Share an HTTPS deep link (https://app.javaschoollab.com/courses/5) configured with Android App Links/iOS Universal Links, handled by the router.

topics.name: Push Notifications and Firebase Cloud Messaging

beginner.content:
How push notifications work

• Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) delivers push messages to Android (and iOS via APNs). Flow: the app gets an FCM registration token → sends it to your Spring Boot server (POST /api/devices, linked to the user) → the server (Firebase Admin SDK for Java) sends a message to a token, a topic (course-updates) or a condition → FCM delivers it → the app shows it and handles the tap.
• Message types: notification messages (FCM displays them automatically when the app is in the background), data messages (custom key-values handled by your code, can wake the app briefly), or both.
• Setup: Firebase project, flutterfire configure, firebase_core + firebase_messaging, Android notification permission (13+), iOS: APNs key in Firebase, capabilities (Push, Background Modes).

intermediate.content:
Sending from Spring Boot

• Add the Firebase Admin SDK (com.google.firebase:firebase-admin), load the service-account credentials from a secret file/environment (never commit it), and keep a device_tokens table (userId, token, platform, lastSeen). Remove tokens that return UNREGISTERED.
• Send by token (personal notifications), by topic (broadcast) or multicast. Put the navigation path in data. Respect user notification settings (store preferences per category) and quiet hours; rate-limit.

expert.content:
Notification UX and reliability

• Android channels let users control categories (create them: "Course updates", "Reminders"); show a rationale before the permission prompt and let users manage preferences in-app. Foreground messages are not shown automatically: display with flutter_local_notifications.
• Reliability: delivery is best-effort; do not rely on push for critical state; keep token registration fresh (on login, token refresh, app start), unregister on logout, and use data + deep link payloads; test on real devices; background handler must be a top-level function.
• Privacy: no sensitive data in the payload; fetch details after the tap.

interviewQA: What is an FCM registration token?

A unique identifier for an app instance on a device that FCM uses to deliver messages. The app sends it to your server, which then targets it (or a topic) when sending notifications; it can change, so listen for refresh.
Why are foreground FCM notifications not shown automatically?
When the app is in the foreground FCM delivers the message to your code (onMessage) instead of the system tray, so you must display it yourself, typically with flutter_local_notifications.
How do you open the right screen from a push?
Send a path in the data payload, and handle getInitialMessage (terminated), onMessageOpenedApp (background) and local notification taps by validating the path and calling the router.

topics.name: Firebase Setup and Firebase Authentication

beginner.content:
Set up Firebase in Flutter

• Firebase is Google's backend-as-a-service: authentication, databases (Firestore, Realtime DB), storage, messaging, analytics, crash reporting, remote config, hosting. Use it next to your Spring Boot backend for what it does best (push, analytics, crash reports, optionally auth), not as a second source of truth for the same data.
• Steps: create a project in the Firebase console → install the CLIs (npm i -g firebase-tools, dart pub global activate flutterfire_cli) → flutterfire configure generates firebase_options.dart (and platform files google-services.json/GoogleService-Info.plist) → flutter pub add firebase_core → await Firebase.initializeApp(options: DefaultFirebaseOptions.currentPlatform) in main(). Use separate Firebase projects for dev and prod.

intermediate.content:
Firebase Authentication

• firebase_auth supports email/password, phone (SMS OTP), anonymous, and federated providers (Google via google_sign_in, Apple, Facebook, GitHub). Enable providers in the console; for Google add the SHA-1/SHA-256 fingerprints of your debug and release keys in project settings.
• API: createUserWithEmailAndPassword, signInWithEmailAndPassword, signInWithCredential, sendPasswordResetEmail, signOut; observe with authStateChanges()/idTokenChanges(); user.getIdToken() returns a JWT you can send to Spring Boot.

expert.content:
Firebase Auth with a Spring Boot backend

• Two designs: (1) Firebase as the identity provider: the app signs in with Firebase, sends await user.getIdToken() as Authorization: Bearer, and Spring Boot verifies the Firebase ID token (Firebase Admin SDK FirebaseAuth.getInstance().verifyIdToken, or configure the JWT resource server with Google's JWKS/issuer https://securetoken.google.com/<project-id>) and maps uid/email to your user; roles live in custom claims or your database. (2) Keep Spring Security's own login (JWT) and use Firebase only for push/analytics: simpler when the web app already uses it.
• Do not trust client-side claims; always verify the token on the server. Refresh: getIdToken() returns a fresh token (cached ~1 h); the Firebase SDK handles refresh.

interviewQA: Why add SHA-1 fingerprints for Google sign-in?
Firebase/Google verify that the sign-in request comes from your signed app by matching the app's signing certificate fingerprint; without the debug and release SHA-1/SHA-256 keys sign-in fails.
How can Spring Boot trust a Firebase user?

The app sends the Firebase ID token; Spring verifies its signature, issuer and audience (Firebase Admin SDK or JWT resource server) and maps the uid/claims to a local user; it must never trust unverified client claims.
authStateChanges vs idTokenChanges?
authStateChanges fires on sign-in and sign-out; idTokenChanges also fires when the ID token is refreshed, useful when you keep the token in memory.

topics.name: Cloud Firestore, Realtime Database, Storage and Security Rules

beginner.content:
Cloud Firestore

• Firestore is a serverless NoSQL document database: collections contain documents (JSON-like maps) that can have subcollections. It supports real-time listeners (snapshots()), queries (where, orderBy, limit, cursors), composite indexes, transactions, batched writes, offline persistence (built in) and security rules.
• Model for your queries (denormalise): no joins. Use typed access with withConverter<T>(fromFirestore, toFirestore). Pricing is per read/write/delete: avoid listening to huge collections; paginate with startAfterDocument.
• Use it for features needing realtime/offline with little backend (chat, live comments, presence); keep core relational data (users, courses, payments) in your Spring Boot + SQL database.

intermediate.content:
Realtime Database and Cloud Storage

• Realtime Database is Firebase's original JSON-tree database with very low-latency listeners (ref.onValue), simple data and presence (.info/connected, onDisconnect). Firestore is usually preferred for richer queries; choose Realtime DB for high-frequency small updates and presence.
• Cloud Storage for Firebase stores user files (images, videos, documents) in Google Cloud Storage buckets: FirebaseStorage.instance.ref('avatars/$uid.jpg').putFile(file) returns an UploadTask with a progress stream; getDownloadURL() gives a tokenised URL. Organise paths per user, set metadata (content type), compress images before upload, and secure with Storage rules.

expert.content:
Firebase Security Rules

• Security rules run on Google's servers and decide who can read/write each document or file: this is your authorisation layer because the app talks to Firebase directly. The default "test mode" (open for 30 days) is dangerous: lock rules before launch.
• Rules see request.auth (uid, token claims), request.resource.data (incoming data), resource.data (existing data). Validate ownership, types, sizes and allowed fields; deny by default; test with the Emulator Suite and @firebase/rules-unit-testing. Use custom claims for roles (request.auth.token.admin == true).

interviewQA: Firestore vs Realtime Database?

Firestore is a document database with richer queries, indexing, scaling and offline support; Realtime Database is a single JSON tree with very low latency, suited to presence and high-frequency small updates.
Why are Firebase security rules critical?
The app accesses Firebase directly, so the rules are the only authorisation layer. Open rules let anyone read or modify your data; use deny-by-default rules that check auth, ownership and data shape.
Should Firestore replace your Spring Boot database?
Not for core relational data. Use it for realtime/offline features (chat, presence) while Spring Boot with SQL remains the source of truth for users, courses and payments.

topics.name: Cloud Messaging, Crashlytics, Analytics and Remote Config

beginner.content:
Crashlytics

• Crashlytics collects crashes and non-fatal errors with stack traces, device and OS info, breadcrumb logs and custom keys, grouped and alerted in the Firebase console. Set up: firebase_crashlytics, Gradle plugin, then forward Flutter errors; upload symbol files for obfuscated builds (--split-debug-info).
• Set the user id (not email) and custom keys (screen, plan), log breadcrumbs (log), record non-fatal exceptions you handle (recordError(..., fatal: false)), and disable collection in debug.

intermediate.content:
Analytics

• Google Analytics for Firebase (firebase_analytics) logs events and user properties: automatic events (first_open, session_start, screen_view with a navigator observer) and custom events (course_enrolled, lesson_completed). Define an event plan (names, parameters) first; limit to 500 distinct events; use snake_case; never log personal data (email, name, phone).
• Get consent where required (GDPR/DPDP): disable collection until accepted (setAnalyticsCollectionEnabled). Use funnels (sign-up → enrol → complete) and audiences in the console; debug with DebugView.

expert.content:
Remote Config and FCM roles

• Remote Config (firebase_remote_config) changes app behaviour and look without a release: feature flags, A/B tests, minimum supported version ("force update"), maintenance mode, promo banners, API base URLs, copy text. Set in-app defaults, fetchAndActivate() with a sensible minimumFetchInterval (12 h in production, 0 in debug), and use conditions (country, app version, user property) and rollouts.
• Cloud Messaging (see the push lesson) delivers notifications; combine: Analytics audiences + FCM topics for targeted campaigns, Remote Config for flags.
• Never put secrets in Remote Config values (they are readable by the app).

interviewQA: What is Crashlytics for?
Real-time crash and non-fatal error reporting with stack traces, device info, custom keys and logs, grouped by issue, so you can find and fix problems users hit in production.
What is Remote Config used for?
Changing app behaviour or content without publishing an update: feature flags, A/B tests, force-update thresholds, maintenance mode and text, with conditions and gradual rollouts.
What should you avoid logging to Analytics?
Personally identifiable information such as email, name or phone number; use anonymous ids and non-personal event parameters, and respect user consent.

topics.name: Unit Testing and Widget Testing

beginner.content:
Unit tests

• Flutter has three test levels: unit (a function/class, no UI, milliseconds), widget (one widget or screen in a simulated environment, no device) and integration (the whole app on a device/emulator). Aim for many unit tests, a good number of widget tests, and a few integration tests (the testing pyramid).
• Add flutter_test (included); files end with _test.dart in test/. Use group, test, setUp, tearDown, expect with matchers (equals, isTrue, throwsA, isA<T>(), closeTo, contains, emitsInOrder for streams). Run with flutter test (--coverage, --name, a single file).

intermediate.content:
Widget tests

• testWidgets('name', (WidgetTester tester) async { ... }): await tester.pumpWidget(MaterialApp(home: MyWidget())) builds the widget; finders (find.text, find.byType, find.byKey, find.byIcon, find.bySemanticsLabel) locate it; interactions (tap, enterText, drag, fling); then pump() (one frame), pump(duration) or pumpAndSettle() (until animations finish); matchers (findsOneWidget, findsNothing, findsNWidgets).
• Wrap the widget in MaterialApp (and ProviderScope/BlocProvider) so Theme, MediaQuery and Navigator exist. Give important widgets Keys. Test behaviour (what the user sees) not widget internals.

expert.content:
Testing async code, timers and layout sizes

• Use tester.runAsync for real async work, fakeAsync + async.elapse(Duration) to control timers/debounce deterministically, and pumpAndSettle only when animations terminate (an infinite animation or spinner makes it time out: use pump with durations).
• Test different screen sizes and text scales: tester.view.physicalSize = const Size(400, 800); addTearDown(tester.view.reset);, and tester.platformDispatcher.textScaleFactorTestValue, to catch overflows. Test accessibility with expectLater(tester, meetsGuideline(androidTapTargetGuideline)) and labeledTapTargetGuideline.
• Keep tests independent, fast and deterministic; no real network, clock or randomness: inject them.

interviewQA: What is the difference between pump and pumpAndSettle?

pump triggers one frame (optionally after a duration); pumpAndSettle keeps pumping until no frames are scheduled (animations finished). With endless animations pumpAndSettle times out; use pump instead.
Why wrap widgets in MaterialApp for tests?
Many widgets need ancestors such as Theme, MediaQuery, Navigator and Directionality that MaterialApp provides; without them tests throw errors.
Unit vs widget vs integration tests?

Unit tests check logic without UI (fast); widget tests build widgets in a simulated environment and interact with them; integration tests run the whole app on a device to verify full flows (slow, few).

topics.name: Integration Testing, Mocking, Golden Tests and Automated Testing

beginner.content:
Mocking

• Replace real dependencies (API, database, clock, platform plugins) with fakes (simple in-memory implementations) or mocks (record and verify calls). Depend on interfaces (abstract interface class CourseRepository) and inject them (constructor or Riverpod overrides), so tests can swap them.
• Packages: mocktail (no code generation, recommended) or mockito (needs build_runner). when(() => repo.fetchAll()).thenAnswer((_) async => courses), verify(() => repo.fetch(1)).called(1), registerFallbackValue for custom argument types.
• Prefer fakes for repositories (simple, readable) and mocks to verify interactions. Mock the network with http_mock_adapter (Dio) or a fake HttpClient.

intermediate.content:
Integration tests

• integration_test (SDK package) runs the real app on a device/emulator and drives it with the same WidgetTester API: login, browse, enrol, offline behaviour. Create integration_test/app_test.dart, call IntegrationTestWidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized(), start the app with app.main() (or pump your root widget with fake services for stable tests), run with flutter test integration_test.
• Point at a test backend (a Spring Boot instance with seeded data) or fake the API layer; keep tests independent (clean state, fresh user).
• Run on a device farm (Firebase Test Lab, BrowserStack, Codemagic) for many devices; record performance with IntegrationTestWidgetsFlutterBinding.traceAction. Alternatives: Patrol (native dialogs, permissions) and Maestro (YAML flows).

expert.content:
Golden tests and test automation

• Golden tests compare a rendered widget against a stored reference image: await expectLater(find.byType(CourseCard), matchesGoldenFile('goldens/course_card.png')). They catch unintended visual changes (spacing, colour, font). Generate or update references with flutter test --update-goldens. Rendering differs across OS/fonts: run goldens on one platform (the CI image), load real fonts (golden_toolkit/alchemist) and keep them small and focused (a component, in light and dark).
• Automation: run dart format --set-exit-if-changed ., flutter analyze, flutter test --coverage and the build on every pull request (GitHub Actions/Codemagic); fail the build on lint errors and coverage drops; upload lcov.info to Codecov. Use coverage as a guide, not a target.

interviewQA: mocktail vs mockito?
Both create mocks to stub and verify calls. mocktail needs no code generation and works with null safety out of the box; mockito requires build_runner generated mocks.
What are golden tests and what is their main pitfall?
They compare a rendered widget with a saved image to catch visual regressions. Pixel output differs across operating systems and fonts, so generate and run them on one consistent platform (CI).
What should run automatically in CI for a Flutter project?
Formatting check, flutter analyze, unit and widget tests with coverage, and a build; integration tests on emulators or a device farm for critical flows.

topics.name: Flutter DevTools, Debugging, Performance Profiling and Memory Leak Detection

beginner.content:
Debugging

• Tools: debugPrint/log (dart:developer; use log(name: ...) for filtering), IDE breakpoints (conditional, logpoints), step through code, inspect variables, exception breakpoints, assert (debug only), debugger(), FlutterError messages (read them: they usually name the cause and fix). Always read the first lines of a red-screen error and the first stack frame in your code.
• Layout bugs: Flutter Inspector (select widget on device, Layout Explorer, constraints), debugPaintSizeEnabled, debugPaintBaselinesEnabled, debugRepaintRainbowEnabled, debugDumpApp(), debugDumpRenderTree(). Network: DevTools Network tab or a proxy (Charles, mitmproxy) / Dio LogInterceptor (debug only).

intermediate.content:
Flutter DevTools and performance profiling

• Open DevTools from the IDE or dart devtools (profile mode for real numbers: flutter run --profile; never profile in debug, it is much slower).
• Tabs: Inspector (widget tree), Performance (frame chart: UI thread and raster thread bars; a frame over 16 ms at 60 fps (8 ms at 120 fps) is janky; look for shader compilation jank and expensive build/layout), CPU Profiler (call tree, flame chart: find hot methods), Memory (heap, allocations, snapshots, GC), Network, Logging, App Size tool, Debugger.
• Flutter performance overlay (showPerformanceOverlay: true) shows two graphs live. Timeline events (Timeline.startSync('parse')) mark your own code. Enable Impeller (default on modern Flutter) for fewer shader compile stutters.

expert.content:
Memory leak detection

• Typical Flutter leaks: undisposed controllers (TextEditingController, AnimationController, ScrollController, FocusNode), uncancelled StreamSubscriptions and Timers, listeners added to long-lived objects and not removed, closures capturing a State/BuildContext, global lists/caches that only grow, large images kept decoded, widgets retained by singletons.
• Detect: DevTools Memory tab: take a snapshot, navigate to the screen and back several times, force GC, take another snapshot and diff (look for instances of your State classes that should be gone); the leak_tracker package (built into flutter_test via LeakTesting) reports undisposed objects in tests; lint close_sinks, cancel_subscriptions.
• Fix: dispose in dispose(), cancel in dispose(), bound caches (LRU), size images (cacheWidth), avoid capturing contexts in long-lived callbacks, use ref.onDispose in Riverpod.

interviewQA: Why profile in profile mode and not debug mode?
Debug builds include assertions and JIT compilation and are far slower, so frame timings are misleading. Profile mode uses AOT-like performance with profiling hooks available.
How do you find a memory leak in a Flutter app?

Use the DevTools Memory tab: snapshot, repeat a navigation flow, force GC, snapshot and diff to find instances (such as a State) that should have been released; also lint for undisposed controllers and uncancelled subscriptions.
What does a janky frame mean?
A frame that takes longer than the frame budget (about 16 ms at 60 Hz), on the UI or raster thread, causing visible stutter; DevTools shows which thread and which work is expensive.

topics.name: Widget Rebuild Optimization, const Constructors, Efficient Lists, Images and Lazy Loading

beginner.content:
Reduce rebuilds

• A rebuild calls build() again: cheap if small, costly if the subtree is big. Optimise what rebuilds, not how often setState is called.
• Techniques: push state down (a small StatefulWidget around the changing part); const constructors (Flutter skips rebuilding identical const instances); extract widget classes (not helper methods); pass a prebuilt child to AnimatedBuilder/ValueListenableBuilder; select only what you need (ref.watch(p.select(...)), context.select, BlocSelector, buildWhen); give widgets stable Keys when reordering; avoid doing work (parsing, sorting, network) in build().
• Use the DevTools "Track widget rebuilds" and debugPrintRebuildDirtyWidgets. Enable lints prefer_const_constructors, prefer_const_literals_to_create_immutables.

intermediate.content:
Efficient list rendering

• Use builder constructors (ListView.builder, GridView.builder, SliverList.builder): only visible items (plus cacheExtent) are built. Never put thousands of items in a plain ListView(children: ...) or a Column inside SingleChildScrollView.
• Give items a key (ValueKey(id)) so state follows the item; set itemExtent/prototypeItem for fixed-height rows (cheaper layout); make item widgets const/small; avoid shrinkWrap: true on long lists; use AutomaticKeepAliveClientMixin only where needed; paginate data (lazy loading) and use RepaintBoundary for complex rows.
• Avoid expensive widgets in rows (Opacity, ClipRRect on large areas, BackdropFilter, shadows with big blur): they trigger saveLayer.

expert.content:
Image optimisation and lazy loading

• Images are the biggest memory and bandwidth cost. Decode at display size: Image.network(url, cacheWidth: 300) / ResizeImage / memCacheWidth in cached_network_image so a 4000 px photo is not decoded fully into memory. Serve appropriately sized, compressed images (WebP/AVIF/JPEG, server-side thumbnails), use cached_network_image for disk/memory caching and placeholders, precacheImage for the next hero, gaplessPlayback to avoid flicker, and vector SVG (flutter_svg) for icons.
• Lazy loading: load data and screens when needed: paginate lists, load tab content when first selected, defer heavy initialisation after the first frame (WidgetsBinding.instance.addPostFrameCallback), deferred components (Android dynamic feature modules) and deferred as libraries on the web.
• Provide placeholder/blur-hash and error widgets for good perceived performance.

interviewQA: Why use const widgets?
A const widget is created once at compile time; when its parent rebuilds Flutter sees the identical instance and skips rebuilding that subtree, saving work.
How do you keep a very long list fast?
Use a builder constructor so only visible items are built, give items keys, use itemExtent for fixed rows, keep item widgets small/const, paginate the data and avoid shrinkWrap.
Why use cacheWidth/memCacheWidth for images?
It decodes the image at the size it is displayed instead of its full resolution, drastically reducing memory use and decode time.

topics.name: Memory Management, Isolate Computation, App Startup, Network and Battery Optimization

beginner.content:
Memory management and isolate-based computation

• Dart is garbage collected; you manage references, not memory: dispose controllers, cancel subscriptions/timers, clear listeners, use bounded caches (LRU), keep large lists paged, ImageCache limits (PaintingBinding.instance.imageCache.maximumSizeBytes), and avoid holding BuildContext beyond its lifetime. Watch memory in DevTools; on low-memory devices respond to didHaveMemoryPressure.
• Move CPU-heavy work to an isolate (Isolate.run, compute): JSON parsing of large payloads, sorting/filtering tens of thousands of items, image processing, encryption, report generation, database bulk inserts (Drift supports NativeDatabase.createInBackground). Rule: anything over ~8 ms per call is a candidate.

intermediate.content:
App startup optimisation

• Measure time to first frame and time to interactive (flutter run --profile --trace-startup, Firebase Performance, Play Console vitals). Targets: cold start under ~2 s on mid-range phones.
• Reduce work before runApp: initialise only what the first screen needs; do the rest after the first frame or lazily (analytics, Crashlytics collection, Remote Config fetch, cache warm-up, SDKs); parallelise independent awaits with Future.wait; avoid synchronous disk reads and big JSON parsing on start; show a native splash (flutter_native_splash) and a skeleton UI immediately.
• Keep the app small: --split-per-abi / app bundles, tree shaking icons (--tree-shake-icons), remove unused packages and assets, compress images, analyse with --analyze-size; smaller binaries load faster.

expert.content:
Network and battery optimisation

• Network: fewer, smaller requests: pagination, request only needed fields, HTTP caching (ETag/If-None-Match, Cache-Control; dio_cache_interceptor), compression (gzip/Brotli on Spring Boot: server.compression.enabled=true), batch calls or combine endpoints (a "home" endpoint), parallel instead of waterfall requests, debounce search, cancel obsolete requests, retry with backoff, offline-first local cache, image CDN with sizes; use HTTP/2.
• Battery: avoid wake locks, continuous GPS/sensors/animations when not visible, polling (use push/FCM or WebSocket instead), frequent background tasks (use WorkManager with constraints and 15+ minute intervals), large uploads on mobile data (prefer Wi-Fi/charging via constraints), unnecessary rebuilds/repaints; pause timers/streams on AppLifecycleState.paused; use dark mode on OLED; reduce animation frame rate where it does not matter (TickerMode, pause off-screen animations).

interviewQA: How do you speed up app startup?

Initialise only what the first screen needs before runApp, run independent initialisation in parallel, move everything else after the first frame or lazily, show a native splash, keep the binary small and measure with --trace-startup.
When should you use an isolate for performance?
For CPU-bound work taking more than a few milliseconds (large JSON parsing, sorting, image or crypto work, bulk database writes) so the UI thread keeps rendering at full frame rate.
How can you reduce battery drain?
Avoid polling and continuous GPS/sensors, use push instead of polling, schedule background work with constraints, pause timers and animations when not visible and batch network requests.

topics.name: Android APK and AAB Builds, iOS Builds and App Signing

beginner.content:
Android builds: APK vs AAB

• APK: installable package (sideloading, testing, direct distribution). AAB (Android App Bundle): the format required by Google Play; Play generates optimised APKs per device (smaller downloads, split by ABI/density/language).
• Commands: flutter build apk --release (or --split-per-abi for per-architecture APKs), flutter build appbundle --release → build/app/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab. Add --obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/symbols (keep symbols for crash reports), --dart-define for config, --flavor prod.
• Before release: set the application id (com.javaschoollab.app), name and icon (flutter_launcher_icons), splash (flutter_native_splash), version, permissions (remove unused), minSdk/targetSdk (Play requires a recent target), and test the release build (behaves differently: minify, no debug).

intermediate.content:
App signing (Android)

• Every Android app must be signed. Create an upload keystore once: keytool -genkey -v -keystore upload-keystore.jks -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000 -alias upload. Reference it from android/key.properties (never commit the keystore or passwords; add to .gitignore; back them up securely).
• Play App Signing (enabled by default for new apps): you sign the AAB with the upload key; Google holds the app signing key and re-signs the APKs delivered to users. If you lose the upload key you can request a reset; with the old model, losing the key meant you could never update the app.
• Register the SHA-1/SHA-256 of the debug, upload and Play app-signing keys with Firebase/Google APIs (Google Sign-In, Maps, App Links).

expert.content:
iOS builds

• Requires a Mac with Xcode and an Apple Developer Program membership (annual fee). Steps: set the bundle identifier, team and signing in Xcode (automatic signing is easiest), add capabilities (Push Notifications, Sign in with Apple, Associated Domains), fill Info.plist usage descriptions, set version/build (CFBundleShortVersionString/CFBundleVersion come from pubspec.yaml).
• Build: flutter build ipa --release (or Xcode: Product → Archive), then upload with Xcode Organizer, xcrun altool/Transporter, or CI (Codemagic, fastlane, GitHub Actions on macOS runners).
• Certificates/profiles: Development and Distribution certificates, provisioning profiles, APNs key for push. fastlane match shares signing assets across a team. TestFlight distributes builds to testers.
codeExamples:
# iOS
cd ios && pod install --repo-update && cd ..
flutter build ipa --release --obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/symbols --export-options-plist=ios/ExportOptions.plist

# upload (App Store Connect API key)
xcrun altool --upload-app --type ios -f build/ios/ipa/javaschoollab.ipa --apiKey <KEY_ID> --apiIssuer <ISSUER_ID>

<!-- ios/Runner/Info.plist -->
<key>NSCameraUsageDescription</key><string>Scan QR codes and take profile photos</string>
<key>NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription</key><string>Choose a profile picture</string>
<key>NSFaceIDUsageDescription</key><string>Unlock the app with Face ID</string>
<key>ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption</key><false/>

interviewQA: APK vs AAB?
An APK is a directly installable package; an AAB is the publishing format required by Google Play, from which Play generates optimised APKs for each device, reducing download size.
What happens if you lose the upload keystore?
With Play App Signing you can ask Google to reset the upload key; without it you could never update the app. Always back up the keystore and passwords securely and never commit them.
What do you need to build for iOS?
A Mac with Xcode, an Apple Developer account, a bundle identifier with signing certificates and provisioning profiles, then flutter build ipa and an upload to App Store Connect/TestFlight.

topics.name: Release Configuration, Play Store and App Store Deployment, Environment Configuration

beginner.content:
Release configuration and environments

• Separate dev, staging and prod: different API URLs, Firebase projects, app ids/names (so all can be installed together) and icons. Mechanisms: flavors (Android product flavors / iOS schemes: flutter run --flavor dev -t lib/main_dev.dart, package flutter_flavorizr), --dart-define-from-file=config/prod.json, and a typed Env class reading String.fromEnvironment.
• Secrets: never commit them; inject from CI secrets. Remember that anything shipped in the app is visible to users; public identifiers are fine, private keys are not.
• Release checklist: version bump, changelog, remove debug banners/logs, test the release build on real devices, enable obfuscation, verify permissions, privacy policy URL, crash reporting enabled, store assets ready.

intermediate.content:
Google Play Store deployment

• One-time: Google Play Console developer account (one-time fee), identity verification. For new personal accounts, closed testing with 12+ testers for 14 days is currently required before production.
• Create the app → complete the store listing (title, short and full description, icon 512x512, feature graphic 1024x500, phone screenshots), content rating questionnaire, target audience, Data safety form (what data you collect/share), privacy policy URL, app access instructions (a test login for reviewers), ads declaration.
• Upload the signed AAB to a track: internal testing (instant, up to 100 testers) → closed → open → production with a staged rollout (5% → 20% → 100%). Check pre-launch reports and Android vitals (crash and ANR rates). Review takes hours to days. Updates need a higher versionCode.
codeExamples:
# pubspec.yaml: bump for every upload   version: 1.3.0+14   (versionName 1.3.0, versionCode 14)

# publish from CI with fastlane supply (Google Play API service account)
fastlane supply --aab build/app/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab --track internal --json_key play-service-account.json
fastlane supply --track_promote_to production --rollout 0.1 --json_key play-service-account.json   # promote with a 10% staged rollout

# Common rejection reasons
# - missing/incorrect Data safety form or privacy policy
# - permissions not justified (SMS, contacts, background location)
# - crashes on launch on reviewer devices (test the RELEASE build)
# - broken login (provide demo credentials in "App access")
# - targetSdk below Google's current requirement

expert.content:
Apple App Store deployment

• Prepare in App Store Connect: create the app record (bundle id), listing (name, subtitle, description, keywords, screenshots for required device sizes, optional preview video), age rating, App Privacy nutrition labels, privacy policy and support URLs, review notes with a demo account.
• Upload the build (Xcode/Transporter/CI) → process → TestFlight (internal testers immediately, external after a quick beta review) → select the build → Submit for Review. Review is typically 24-48 hours. Choose phased release for gradual rollout.
• Frequent rejections: crashes, placeholder content, login needed without a demo account, missing account deletion flow (required if you offer sign-up), Sign in with Apple required when offering other social logins, unjustified permissions/tracking (App Tracking Transparency), payments: digital goods must use in-app purchase, incomplete metadata. Respect Apple's Human Interface Guidelines.
codeExamples:
# Release checklist (both stores)
# [ ] version and build number bumped
# [ ] release build tested on real devices (cold start, login, push, deep links, offline)
# [ ] crash reporting (Crashlytics) enabled and symbols uploaded
# [ ] API pointing to PRODUCTION, debug logging off
# [ ] privacy policy, Data safety / App Privacy forms accurate
# [ ] account deletion available (Apple/Google requirement for apps with sign-up)
# [ ] demo credentials in review notes
# [ ] store screenshots, description, icon, age rating done
# [ ] backend ready for load (Spring Boot scaled, rate limits, monitoring)
# [ ] staged rollout planned, rollback plan (previous build) ready

interviewQA: How do you manage dev, staging and production configuration in Flutter?
Use flavors (separate app ids, names, Firebase projects) together with --dart-define or --dart-define-from-file read through a typed Env class, injecting secrets from CI rather than committing them.
What is a staged rollout?
Releasing an update to a percentage of users first (for example 10%) and increasing it as crash and vitals metrics stay healthy, so a bad release affects fewer people and can be halted.
Why do apps with sign-up need an account deletion feature?
Both Google Play and the Apple App Store require that users can initiate deletion of their account and data from within the app (and a web link), as part of privacy policy compliance.

topics.name: CI/CD Pipelines, Version Management and Crash Monitoring

beginner.content:
Version management

• version: 1.3.0+14 in pubspec.yaml: 1.3.0 is the user-visible version name (semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH); 14 is the build number (versionCode on Android, CFBundleVersion on iOS), which must increase on every store upload. Override on the command line: --build-name=1.3.0 --build-number=$GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER.
• Tag releases in Git (v1.3.0), keep a CHANGELOG (Conventional Commits help), and plan forced/recommended updates (Remote Config minimum version, in_app_update on Android, App Store link on iOS) because old app versions keep calling your API: version your API (/api/v1) and stay backward compatible.

intermediate.content:
CI/CD pipelines

• CI: on every PR run format check, flutter analyze, tests with coverage, and a build. CD: on tags/merge to main build the signed AAB/IPA and upload to Play internal testing and TestFlight, then promote after QA.
• Tools: GitHub Actions (Android on Linux, iOS on macOS runners), Codemagic (Flutter-focused, handles iOS signing and store publishing), fastlane (lanes for build/sign/upload), Bitrise, Jenkins (self-hosted). Store the keystore (base64), passwords and service-account JSON as encrypted secrets; never print them. Cache pub packages; fail fast.
codeExamples:
# .github/workflows/release-android.yml
name: Release Android
on:
  push: { tags: ['v*'] }
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: 17 }
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { channel: stable, cache: true }
      - run: flutter pub get
      - run: flutter analyze --fatal-infos && flutter test
      - name: Restore signing key
        run: |
          echo "${{ secrets.UPLOAD_KEYSTORE_BASE64 }}" | base64 --decode > android/upload-keystore.jks
          printf 'storePassword=%s\nkeyPassword=%s\nkeyAlias=upload\nstoreFile=../upload-keystore.jks\n' "${{ secrets.KEYSTORE_PASSWORD }}" "${{ secrets.KEY_PASSWORD }}" > android/key.properties
      - run: flutter build appbundle --release --build-number=${{ github.run_number }} --dart-define-from-file=config/prod.json --obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/symbols
      - uses: r0adkll/upload-google-play@v1
        with:
          serviceAccountJsonPlainText: ${{ secrets.PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON }}
          packageName: com.javaschoollab.app
          releaseFiles: build/app/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab
          track: internal
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: symbols, path: build/symbols }

expert.content:
Crash monitoring and release health

• Crashlytics/Sentry give crash-free users/sessions, new vs regressed issues, affected versions/devices and breadcrumbs. Upload obfuscation symbols (firebase crashlytics:symbols:upload, sentry_dart_plugin) from CI so stack traces are readable. Add the release version to every report.
• Also watch Play Console Android vitals (crash rate, ANR rate, startup time, battery) and App Store Connect crash reports; set alerts (a regression after a rollout should page someone), and halt the staged rollout when crash-free sessions drop below your threshold (for example 99.5%).
• Close the loop: triage new issues daily, link them to tickets, ship hotfixes (patch versions) quickly, use Remote Config kill switches for broken features, and monitor the Spring Boot side (Actuator, logs with request ids) so mobile and server errors can be correlated.

interviewQA: What is the difference between version name and build number?
The version name (1.3.0) is shown to users and follows semantic versioning; the build number (versionCode/CFBundleVersion) is an integer that must increase with every store upload.
Why version the backend API when you ship a mobile app?
Installed app versions cannot all be updated at once, so older apps keep calling the API; versioned and backward-compatible endpoints prevent breaking them.
Why upload debug symbols for obfuscated builds?
Obfuscation renames symbols; without the symbol files crash stack traces in Crashlytics/Sentry are unreadable and hard to debug.

topics.name: Projects 1-5: Calculator, To-Do, Weather, Notes and Expense Tracker

beginner.content:
1. Calculator app (beginner)

• Skills: layout (GridView/Row/Column), setState, string/number logic, expression parsing, responsive buttons, unit tests.
• Features: digits, + - × ÷, clear, backspace, decimal, percent, divide-by-zero handling, history. Keep the calculation logic in a pure class (testable) separate from the UI.

intermediate.content:
2. To-Do app and 3. Weather app

• To-Do (state + persistence): add, edit, complete, delete (swipe with Dismissible), filter (all/active/done), reorder (ReorderableListView), due dates, persistence with Drift/Hive/SharedPreferences, Riverpod AsyncNotifier, undo SnackBar. Optional: sync with a Spring Boot /api/tasks.
• Weather (API + async): call a public API (Open-Meteo is free without a key), model JSON, show current + 7-day forecast, search city (geocoding), current location (geolocator), loading/error/empty states, pull-to-refresh, cache last result for offline, unit toggle (°C/°F), icons by weather code.

expert.content:
4. Notes app and 5. Expense tracker

• Notes (database + search): create/edit/delete notes with title/body/colour/pinned, full-text search (SQLite FTS5 via Drift), tags, auto-save (debounced), trash/restore, markdown preview, share, backup/export, and a simple sync later.
• Expense tracker (data + charts): add expenses (amount, category, date, note), monthly totals, charts (fl_chart: pie by category, bar by day), budgets with alerts, filters by month/category, CSV export, currency formatting (intl), recurring expenses (WorkManager/local notifications), Drift with aggregation queries.

interviewQA: What does a calculator project teach?
Layout with grids, state handling, separating pure business logic from UI, edge cases (decimals, division by zero) and unit testing.
Which free weather API needs no key?
Open-Meteo provides current and forecast data without an API key; it is ideal for practice projects.
How do you build charts for an expense tracker?
Aggregate data with SQL group-by queries (Drift) and feed the totals into fl_chart widgets such as PieChart and BarChart.

topics.name: Projects 6-7: Login and Registration App, E-Commerce Application

beginner.content:
6. Login and registration app (with Spring Boot)

• Skills: forms, validation, Dio, Spring Security JWT, secure storage, token refresh, GoRouter guards, error handling, Riverpod.
• Screens: splash (restore session) → login → register → verify email (optional) → forgot password → home/profile → logout. Features: show/hide password, autofill, biometric re-login, remember me, field-level server errors, loading buttons, deep link for password reset.
• Spring Boot endpoints: /api/auth/register, /login, /refresh, /logout, /forgot-password, /reset-password, /me; BCrypt hashing, validation, rate limiting, refresh-token rotation.

intermediate.content:
7. E-commerce application

• Skills: product catalogue (grid + search + filters + pagination), product detail (carousel, variants, reviews), cart (state, quantity, persistence), checkout (address form, shipping, payment), orders history/tracking, wishlist, auth, push notifications for order status, offline cache, deep links to products.
• Payments: never handle raw card data; use a gateway SDK (Razorpay, Stripe, PayPal): the server creates an order/PaymentIntent, the app confirms payment with the SDK, the server verifies the result via webhook (the client's "success" is not proof). Make order creation idempotent.
• Backend (Spring Boot): products, cart/orders, inventory checks in a transaction (@Transactional, optimistic locking), price computed on the server (never trust client prices), order status workflow, webhooks.

expert.content:
Screens, architecture and extras

• Navigation: bottom bar (Home, Categories, Cart, Orders, Profile) with StatefulShellRoute; deep links /products/:id; hero transition from list to detail.
• Architecture: feature folders, repositories, Riverpod, Dio with auth interceptor, Drift cache for catalogue and cart, cached_network_image, skeleton loaders (shimmer), error/empty states.
• Production: analytics funnel (view → add to cart → checkout → purchase), crash reporting, remote config for banners/flags, FCM for order updates, accessibility, localisation (intl, ARB files), tests (cart logic unit tests, widget tests for checkout, integration test for purchase with a fake gateway).

interviewQA: Why must the server compute prices in an e-commerce app?
Clients can be modified, so any price, discount or total sent by the app is untrusted. The server must look up prices and compute totals from its own data.
How should payments be confirmed?

The server creates the payment order, the app completes it with the gateway SDK, and the server confirms the final status through the gateway webhook; the client's success callback alone is not proof of payment.
What should the login app do on start?
Show a splash while restoring the session from secure storage and calling /api/me, then route to home if valid or to login if not, using router redirects.

topics.name: Projects 8-10: Chat Application, Online Quiz Application and Learning Management System

beginner.content:
8. Chat application

• Skills: real-time streams, message list UI, optimistic sending, presence/typing, media messages, push notifications, offline queue.
• Backends: Firebase (Firestore listeners + FCM + Storage; quickest) or Spring Boot WebSocket/STOMP (own server; integrates with your user database). Features: 1-1 and group chats, unread counts, read receipts, image sharing, message pagination (older messages on scroll), reconnect, notifications when backgrounded, end-to-end encryption (advanced).
• UI: reversed ListView (reverse: true) so new messages appear at the bottom; message bubbles aligned by sender; auto-scroll when at bottom; date separators.

intermediate.content:
9. Online quiz application

• Skills: state machines, timers, animations, scoring, API + local fallback, charts.
• Flow: choose course/topic → load questions (random N, difficulty) → one question per screen (PageView or state-driven) with a countdown timer (Timer.periodic/TweenAnimationBuilder) → answer feedback → results (score, time, correct/incorrect review, share) → leaderboard and history.
• Design: model quiz state as a sealed class (NotStarted, InProgress(index, answers, remaining), Finished(score)); keep scoring on the server for fairness (the app sends answers, the server returns the score; never ship correct answers in the payload for graded quizzes); anti-cheating basics (time limit enforced server-side, shuffle options, one attempt).

expert.content:
10. Learning Management System: the JavaSchoolLab mobile app

• This is the capstone: a Flutter client for the existing JavaSchoolLab platform, reusing its Spring Boot API, accounts and content.
• Features: login (JWT, biometric unlock), course catalogue and search, course detail with modules/topics, lesson reader (render HTML lessons with flutter_widget_from_html, code blocks with syntax highlighting and copy button, offline downloads), progress tracking (mark topics complete, resume where you left off, sync), quizzes and certificates (PDF download/share), bookmarks and notes, dark mode, offline mode (Drift cache, sync queue), push notifications (new lessons, streak reminders via FCM), deep links (/course/java/topic), analytics, crash reporting, localisation.
• Architecture: Flutter + Riverpod + GoRouter + Dio + Drift + secure storage + FCM; Spring Boot (Java 21) REST API with Spring Security JWT, PostgreSQL/MySQL; CI/CD with GitHub Actions to Play internal testing; Crashlytics + Remote Config.

interviewQA: How would you design the LMS mobile app's offline support?

Cache courses and downloaded lessons in a Drift database, read the UI from the database, record progress locally and queue it for sync with idempotent actions, and pull server changes since the last sync.
Why score quizzes on the server?
The client can be modified, so grading and time limits must be enforced by the backend; the app sends answers and receives the result, and graded questions should not expose correct answers.
What technology stack would you use for the JavaSchoolLab Flutter app?

Flutter and Dart with Riverpod, GoRouter, Dio, Drift and secure storage, FCM for notifications, talking to the existing Spring Boot REST API with Spring Security JWT and a PostgreSQL/MySQL database, deployed through CI/CD to Google Play.

cheatNotes: Widget - The basic building block of every Flutter UI element
StatelessWidget - Immutable widget with no internal mutable state
StatefulWidget - Widget backed by a State object that can change via setState()
setState() - Notifies Flutter to rebuild a StatefulWidget subtree

Row / Column - Arrange children horizontally / vertically
Container - Box-model widget for padding, margin, decoration, sizing
Expanded / Flexible - Make a child fill or share available space in a Row/Column
ListView.builder - Efficiently builds a long/infinite scrollable list on demand
Hot Reload - Injects updated code into a running app in under a second
Hot Restart - Restarts the app fresh, resetting all state
pubspec.yaml - Declares dependencies, assets, and fonts for a Flutter project
MaterialApp / CupertinoApp - Root widget providing Android / iOS style theming
Navigator.push() / pop() - Push a new route onto / pop the top route off the stack
Provider - Popular package for sharing and rebuilding on state changes
ChangeNotifier - Class that can notify listeners when its data changes
context.watch<T>() - Subscribes to rebuilds when T changes (used in build())
context.read<T>() - Reads T once without subscribing (used in callbacks)
Future / async / await - Dart's building blocks for asynchronous code
FutureBuilder - Rebuilds UI based on a Future's loading/error/data state
StreamBuilder - Rebuilds UI based on events from a Stream
const constructor - Marks a widget as compile-time constant for better performance
Key - Identifies widgets across rebuilds, important for list item state
